This refined model is then used to calculate phonon densities of states and dispersion for several systems and demonstrates significant improvements over existing methods.

Building upon our prior findings regarding WSTS with finite sets, we've found a way to establish that for WSTS with finite sets, we can replace "forward termination" with "reachability in a finite number of steps", and "upward closure" with "a finite accumulation point exists". To prove this, we've established a specific type of decidable verification for WSTS with Karp-Miller forests. This decidable verification involves a "sub-capture" relation, which is a weakened capture relation, to facilitate this verification. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that any decidable verification for WSTS that utilizes Karp-Miller forests can be transformed into one utilizing the sub-capture relation, which is the basis for our main theorem.

The 4th International Fermi Symposium was held in Bonn, Germany, from October 9-12, 2015. I attended and presented my work through a poster, utilizing it to showcase a novel tool for generating a comprehensive, dynamic map of gamma-ray sky data collected by the Fermi-LAT over 10 years. This map was produced by merging machine learning models with the standard 4-year Fermi-LAT energy map, and was created using a classification system that applied convolutional neural networks to identify sources as permanent, temporary, or variable. I also showcased how this map can be used to pinpoint sources that change over time, and demonstrated its potential by identifying a group of sources that show increased activity at high galactic latitudes during specific periods.

A key feature of traditional theories is that they operate based on pre-assumed concepts without justifying their initial assumptions. This paper explores the potential of alternative explanations rooted in fundamental principles rather than assumptions. A proposed approach for deriving fundamental laws is presented, which emphasizes the importance of the underlying model's inherent properties. This method is then applied to the most basic model of reality, which is just a single point in space and time. This approach is similar to the idea of fundamentalism, but it differs in that it prioritizes the fundamental laws over the underlying model. A proposed framework for deriving fundamental laws is presented, which is based on the idea of 'processes' rather than 'things'. This framework is applied to the concept of causation, which is seen as a fundamental principle that is more fundamental than the underlying laws of physics. This approach is then applied to the study of the emergence of classical reality from a quantum universe, which is seen as a fundamental principle that is more fundamental than the underlying laws of physics.

This research paper presents a set of infinite limits that build upon the Auerbach invariants of three-dimensional geometric objects with bounded coordinates, and includes a review of the historical development of these invariants and their role in generalizing the properties of convex polyhedra.

Tabular data, such as those found in datasets like Adult and CoverType, consist of organized tables with multiple columns that provide valuable insights into real-world settings, making them crucial for various applications. Recent breakthroughs in neural networks have significantly improved performance in text and image tasks, with a growing need for similar advancements in structured tabular data, such as that found in linear models and decision trees. To address this, we have developed a new framework called Structured Attention Network for Tabular Input, or SAINT, which incorporates row-level attention and contrastive pre-training to enhance performance. Through our approach, we demonstrate substantial improvements in performance on diverse tabular datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art models and yielding significant increases in accuracy, driven by the effectiveness of our attention and contrastive methods, as well as our ability to effectively capture feature interactions.

As wireless channels fluctuate with time and space, ensuring reliable communication requires adaptive channel estimation. A novel solution called random forest (RF) deep learning has been proposed to estimate channels in time-selective and frequency-flat wireless networks. This study investigates the performance of RF for channel estimation in various wireless environments. The performance of RF is compared to traditional linear minimum mean square error estimators across different network settings and signal-to-noise ratios. A deep learning framework with multiple hyperparameters makes it challenging to determine the most effective settings. To overcome this issue, a method is presented that utilizes synthetic data to efficiently train random forest models, allowing for the use of simulated data without requiring extensive training datasets. The results demonstrate that RF provides better estimation accuracy than linear estimators, especially in more complex networks. The proposed hyperparameter selection method also ensures the use of RF models with the highest possible accuracy.

In gauge theories, the center vortex model offers an appealing explanation for the confinement phenomenon but encounters an obstruction known as the Gribov issue. To address this problem, we developed a novel approach that reinterprets the issue as a multidimensional minimization problem in coordinate space and employs cutting-plane refinements to navigate the complex landscape. Our method successfully yields stable, reliable configurations, which we have dubbed "core regions." These core regions serve as a stable foundation for expressing physical gauge fields in a way that satisfies both the issue and the criteria for confinement within the center vortex model.

We've examined how the destruction of dark matter affects the luminosity of low-surface-brightness galaxies (LSBGs)), specifically in relation to the presence of star formation. We utilized the Dark Energy Survey's Y3 data, which allowed us to analyze the luminosity distribution of LSLGs without relying on specific models. We discovered that the luminosity function of LSLGs doesn't change significantly over time. We then used a statistical approach to constrain the destruction rate of dark matter in LSLGs, which would reduce their luminosity, under the assumption that this rate is constant and uniform. Our results indicate that the destruction rate must be less than 0.64 at a 68% confidence level, suggesting that dark matter destruction is unlikely to play a major role in shaping the luminosity distribution of LSLGs.

Our goal in this research is to enhance the quality of search results by modifying
search queries through automatic query rephrasing. This process involves identifying
key concepts and their respective weights from user queries. To achieve this, our
system analyzes a large number of queries related to a particular topic and tracks
the frequency of specific terms. This enables our system to determine the importance
of each word and its relevance to the original query. To evaluate our approach, we
have collected a large dataset consisting of over 1.8 million search queries and used
it to test our system against a widely recognized benchmark. The results show that our
method performs significantly better than existing solutions, with an F1 score of 0.73
and an average improvement in the number of relevant documents retrieved per search
query of 246.84%.

We've proposed a novel algorithmic approach to efficiently solve large systems of Darcy flows with variable properties across multiple areas. By breaking down the system into smaller, interconnected sub-domain systems and deriving a pre-conditioning technique from these smaller systems, we've developed a method that remains effective even when certain parameters change within a significant range. This approach allows for easy adaptation to handle changes in the number of sub-domains or changes in the structure of these sub-domains. Furthermore, we've developed a method to predict and correct for inaccuracies in the initial pre-conditioning estimate, ensuring a reduction in the complexity of the problem by several orders of magnitude.

Summarizing multi-turn conversations is a difficult task because it demands not only identifying the most important information but also capturing the logical connections between the different statements. Previous approaches to this problem focused on generating summaries from individual turns, but this method is limiting because it fails to consider the relationships between the turns and often includes extraneous information in its output. To overcome this, we propose a novel approach to this problem that first identifies these connections and then uses them to organize the information in a way that makes it easier to create a summary. Our approach involves using a pre-trained model to identify the connections between the turns in a conversation and then using a simple organization system to group the most important information together. Our experiments show that this method significantly outperforms previous approaches to this problem.

A cutting-edge deep learning model has been developed to forecast the widening of the Doppler bandwidth resulting from cross-section distributions for complex radar targets. This model leverages a combination of physical and geometric attributes, including the number of targets, target cross-section size, radar frequency, and beamwidth. The proposed neural network employs a combination of fully connected and convolutional layers to learn complex relationships and estimate cross-section influence on Doppler bandwidth. To validate the approach, numerical simulations were conducted using a full-wave method to calculate radar cross-sections. The proposed model's accuracy was evaluated through root mean square error and R-squared metrics, yielding 0.9 and 97% respectively. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a physically-inspired deep learning framework in estimating the widening of Doppler bandwidth caused by complex radar cross-section distributions.

This study begins by developing a new method to create n-Lie algebras. It then focuses on specific types of n-Lie algebras and their associated structures, known as pre-Lie algebras. By using a unique, tree-like decomposition process, we can transform an n-Lie algebra into a pre-Lie algebra in a way that preserves its original structure. Furthermore, we show that the resulting pre-Lie algebra has a distinct 'tree decomposition' that is closely related to its 2-nary bracket matrix. Additionally, we establish a connection between pre-Lie algebras and dendrification of n-Lie algebras, which involves a generalization of a tree decomposition process.

Cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-mMIMO) technology holds promise in enhancing future mobile networks. In this study, we investigate how a cell-free geometry-based modeling approach can be used to evaluate average quality of service in downlink cell-free massive MIMO systems. We analyze the average rate of users in a Poisson-distributed network of scatterers to determine the minimum required transmit power for a specified coverage probability. We also explore how various system parameters such as base station density, user density, antenna array size, and path loss exponent affect the average rate and minimum required power in cell-free systems compared to traditional multi-cell geometry-based MIMO systems. Our results demonstrate that by adjusting specific system parameters, we can achieve a balance between the coverage probability and required power in cell-free systems.

Given a sequence of complex numbers $\{c_n\}$ and a sequence of natural numbers $\{r_n\}$, and defining the sequence of complex numbers $\{P_{n-m}$\}$ for some positive integer $m$, we examine the convergence of the series $\sum_{j=0}^{m} c_{n-j} P_j$ when $j$ is less than or equal to $n-m$, and show that this series converges uniformly for all $n$ greater than or equal to 1 to the expression $\sum_{j=0}^m c_{n-j} P_j$ evaluated at $n$, provided that the sequence $\{c_{n-j}\}_{j=0}^{m}$ converges as $n$ goes to infinity, and some additional mild conditions are met.

Understanding the mechanical characteristics of disordered materials is crucial for accurately predicting their behavior during industrial applications and technological advancements. A major obstacle in this understanding lies in the intricate relationship between a material's static arrangement and its dynamic response to external stress. Our study focuses on a specific type of plastic polymer, a type of glassy material composed of spherical particles, to explore the connections between its internal structure, its memory, and its overall dynamics. Our results show that the material's ability to remember its initial state is heavily influenced by the stress it has been subjected to and the rate at which it has been subjected to that stress. Furthermore, we discovered that the material's memory and its internal structure are inextricably linked, and that the material's overall dynamics can be described by a combination of these two properties. These findings provide new insights into the complex behavior of glassy materials under stress, shedding light on how they respond to and remember past deformations.

The objective of ongoing object detection is to continuously identify objects in video streams without stopping, making it indispensable for applications like self-driving vehicles. This paper examines various definitions and algorithms of ongoing object detection, examines its distinctive characteristics, discusses difficulties in its implementation, and explores its applications across different sectors. We also compare prominent models of ongoing object detection and assess their performance based on standard evaluation criteria, ultimately discussing future trends in this field.

The BDMPS-Z formalism is employed to investigate the modification of the gluon splitting function $g\rightarrow c\bar{c}$ within the context of medium formed by heavy quark-antiquark pairs. The incorporation of the complex binding energy due to a Coulomb potential is crucial in deriving the modified gluon spectral function and the probability of gluon conversion into a $c\bar{c}$ pair. The outcomes of our analysis reveal that the binding energy significantly amplifies the conversion probability of gluons into $c\bar{c}$ pairs in comparison to the conversion into light quarks. Additionally, we have determined the probability density function of $c\bar{c}$ pairs within the quark-antiquark system.

Deep neural networks often struggle to apply what they've learned to new, unseen environments, but when we have enough data from those new environments, we can improve performance on that data.  Unfortunately, gathering that new data can be time-consuming and expensive.  Domain adaptation techniques can help bridge the gap, but only to a limited extent.  A new approach called domain generalization aims to enable a model to perform well in entirely new, unrelated environments, without needing to train on that new data.  Our research focuses on improving domain generalization by integrating interpretability methods.  We've developed an information-theoretic metric that quantifies how well a model's features capture the underlying data patterns, and we've used this metric to drive the selection of the most effective domain-invariant representations.  Our experiments show that incorporating this metric into the model selection process significantly enhances performance in novel environments, surpassing even the strong baseline of our best existing model.

The Internet's infrastructure is comprised of diverse, interconnected networks with varying characteristics. This leads to distinct communication requirements and challenges among different networks. Focusing on networks with limited internet infrastructure, we're investigating efficient methods for agent interaction. To this end, we're developing a blockchain-based system that enhances security, monitoring, and collaboration among entities within networks with limited internet connectivity.

Our analysis focuses on the alpha-attraction model, a cosmological theory characterized by complex dynamics. By employing the slow-roll approximation, we have derived the inflationary power spectrum P(P), and introduced the alpha-inflation model to match observational data. We have also developed a simplified parameterization, alpha-deformed P(P), which allows for a more straightforward evaluation of the spectral index n_s and its running. Our analysis utilizes the Planck 2018 dataset and forecasts future BICEP/Keck and LSS constraints. We have identified two distinct inflationary configurations, and introduced the alpha-configuration, which offers a more compelling fit to the data. Our findings suggest that the alpha-attraction model can effectively explain current observational results.

This paper outlines innovative methods for optimizing end-to-end artificial intelligence workflows on Intel Xeon processors, primarily focusing on the key components that make up these workflows. We will be detailing strategies for enhancing training and inference phases using both CPU and HPC resources, as well as optimizing data preparation activities. We will also be presenting findings from implementing these techniques to inform future workflow design.

The paper re-examines the relationships between the Bayes factor, HDI-ROPE, and equivalence testing, demonstrating that these quantities can be derived from one another using specific formulas, depending on the chosen equivalence threshold. By applying these formulas, Bayes factors and HDI-ROPE values can be converted to one another, while the equivalence probability can be determined from the Bayes factor. Furthermore, the paper presents a novel approach to interpreting equivalence probabilities within a Bayesian framework.

A new language transmission system called the VQ-semantic transmission system has been proposed, which can reduce semantic and channel coding overhead. In this system, input sequences are first encoded using an autoencoder, which produces a compressed semantic representation. A vector quantization process then encodes this representation for more efficient transmission. Unlike conventional methods that only reduce the number of symbols sent, the VQ-semantic transmission system also decreases the number of unique semantic vectors stored, resulting in further reductions during channel coding. Furthermore, the system demonstrates significant gains in bit error rate performance, particularly when the initial autoencoder layer has a relatively low channel coding rate. Notably, the proposed method's ability to decrease the number of stored vectors is limited by the size of the encoded data, with a minimum threshold.

As the global Data volume continues to escalate, a new challenge has arisen in the form of an overwhelming data analysis burden. To overcome this issue, a novel framework is proposed that integrates the capabilities of multi-objective evolutionary algorithms and neural networks to provide a dynamic, adaptive, and result-oriented analytics solution. This framework differs from conventional approaches in its ability to adapt dynamically based on changing user preferences and goal objectives. Furthermore, a unique analytical process is proposed that enhances insights by leveraging the synergy between various services operating on both structured and unstructured data sets.

This work delves into a specific type of category theory, called a doctrina, which extends beyond the conventional category by incorporating an additional framework that can be further refined using a specific type of concept known as a comonad. We will explore the relationship between these two ideas and discuss how a doctrina can be effectively utilized with a particular type of comonad known as a dual comonad. The idea is that the comonad can be used to create a framework within the doctrina that can be utilized to create a new concept known as a method. We will explore the relationship between these ideas and discuss how a doctrina can be used to create a foundation for such a concept. We will also examine the idea of a dual comonad and discuss how it can be used to create a new concept known as a comorphism.

A novel Bayesian nonparametric method, known as graphically assistant clustered network autoregression model (GACNAR), is introduced to uncover hidden graph structures in network data and develop tailored predictive models for each cluster. The proposed framework utilizes a Dirichlet process mixture regression model within each cluster, allowing the selection of a kernel from a predefined set of options. The Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Model (DPMG) serves as a base model, offering a suitable starting point. The GACNAR model incorporates a stick-breaking Dirichlet mixture kernel to ensure that the selected kernels are unique within each cluster. The proposed method also incorporates a Dirichlet prior distribution to account for similarities among clusters, thereby facilitating the identification of clusters. The GACNAR model's parameters are estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations, with the predictive ability of each kernel evaluated based on the posterior probability of future observations. The proposed method is applied to two datasets: a simulated network autoregressive model and a financial dataset. The results demonstrate the GACNAR model's ability to accurately identify clusters, develop effective predictive models, and yield higher predictive accuracy compared to a univariate autoregressive model.

A significant issue in applying artificial intelligence to various tasks, such as reading comprehension, is the disparity between the amount of training and testing data available. This disparity is particularly pronounced in domains like biology and history, where creating annotated data is resource-intensive. To address this challenge, our proposed model, RerrFact, utilizes fine-tuned evidence retrieval representations to enhance performance in domain-specific information-seeking tasks, achieving comparable results with less data. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated on the HAC dataset for scientific hypothesis generation, showcasing improved performance in a semi-sparse setting using only 20% of the original data.

This study presents an innovative automated system for categorizing and isolating posterior segment OCT images. Its key capabilities include automatically categorizing images into normal and diseased groups, as well as identifying and isolizing individual images within each group. To achieve this, we employed a novel segmentation method known as the "grow and subdivide" approach, which leverages a real-time analysis tool to isolate the posterior segment. We also developed a sophisticated classification model that integrates multiple features and uses a combination of classifiers to achieve precise results. We tested our system using a dataset of 300 posterior segment OCT images, 150 of which were normal and 150 affected by various conditions. We conducted rigorous testing on our system, comparing its performance with existing methods and evaluating its robustness to different feature combinations and classifiers. We found that our system exhibited high accuracy, with a classification rate of 92.67% and an area under the curve of 0.96, and significantly outperformed other methods in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and AUC.

The brain's ability to process information efficiently is thought to be a critical factor in cognitive flexibility, but the way it achieves this efficiency is still not well understood. Researchers have proposed the superstatistical framework as a possible explanation, suggesting that the brain's neural networks operate by switching between different modes of information processing. However, this approach assumes a fixed number of modes, limiting its ability to accurately model complex neural behavior. In contrast, we propose a new method called neural superstatistics that uses Bayesian inference to estimate the number of modes and how they change over time, without making any assumptions. This method is applied to brain activity data from humans and rhesus macaques, demonstrating its ability to detect dynamic changes in cognitive flexibility and identify the different modes of information processing.

This research paper proposes an explicit formula to identify Mersenne prime numbers. It's worth noting that the proposed formula conflicts with existing knowledge on the distribution of Mersenne primes, raising questions about its underlying implications.

Hilbert's sixth problem concerns the universal underlying principles that govern the behavior of dissipative hydrodynamic systems resulting from the kinetic theory of gases. This problem has been divided into two sub-problems, one focusing on the dynamics of surface gravity waves and the other on the dynamics of the fluids themselves. The dynamics of surface gravity waves have been shown to be governed by a single variable, the fluid's vertical distance from the surface, and this is consistent with the findings of Selinger. The dynamics of the fluids themselves are more complex, with multiple variables, including fluid velocity, temperature, and surface tension, all influencing one another. The dynamics of these fluids are governed by a set of equations, with fluid velocity and temperature playing central roles, and this is consistent with the findings of Ziegler. The implications of these findings are significant, with the discovery of a universal underlying principle governing the behavior of a wide range of systems, from the dynamics of fluid surfaces to the dynamics of fluid flows, and this is independent of the specific details of the systems being studied.

The molecular gas in galaxies is primarily composed of cold atomic and ionized components, with atomic gas (specifically, neutral atoms) serving as an indicator of the reservoir of molecular gas. The emission from this atomic gas can be used to study the physical conditions within the gas. We have compiled existing data on the emission from interstellar atomic gas in local galaxies, along with theoretical calculations based on local thermodynamic equilibrium assumptions, to compare observed line ratios with those predicted by these assumptions. The analysis reveals that the emission from atomic gas in galaxies cannot be explained by thermal processes, given the observed line ratios. Instead, it appears to be the result of subthermal stimulation, with our calculations indicating that this subthermal stimulation can account for the observed line ratios. Furthermore, we have found that the ratio of specific lines in atomic gas emission can be used to estimate the temperature of the gas. This temperature estimate can be used to constrain models of molecular gas chemistry and the rate of molecular hydrogen formation.

This research paper describes the challenges and outcomes of creating a treebank
for spoken language analysis of code-switching data, particularly for spoken
Dutch and Frisian. A novel corpus is presented, consisting of 10 hours of audio
recordings in spoken Dutch and Frisian, as well as their code-switched version.
The corpus annotations include speech recognition transcripts, morphological
analyses, and structural tree diagrams in the UD Franplatter treebank.

The process of photoevaporation, which occurs when a star's UV radiation strips away its surrounding disk material, plays a significant role in determining a disk's lifespan and the formation of planets. Although it's known that photoevaporation is influenced by the star's mass, the extent of this effect remains unclear. Researchers have employed a combination of observations and models to investigate how a star's mass impacts the formation of protoplanetary disks. By analyzing data from the Spitzer Space Telescope, the team discovered that higher-mass young stars possess larger disks, while those surrounding lower-mass stars experience slower disk evolution. By modeling these systems, the team found that photoevaporation rates are indeed affected by a star's mass, leading to the formation of hot, inner disks and cold, outer disks. This mass-dependent photoevaporation process can significantly influence the initial structure of the disk and may ultimately result in the formation of planet-forming disks.

The incorporation of the $\alpha$ method within isogeometric analysis, utilizing generalized-$\alpha$ techniques, has been successful in enhancing the accuracy of structural dynamics simulations by achieving higher order of spatial and temporal accuracy. Nevertheless, the need for additional parameters to apply this method in structural dynamics simulations results in a trade-off between computational efficiency and accuracy. This study presents a new approach to isogeometric structural dynamics by combining the $\alpha$ method with a new scheme for determining the $\alpha$ parameter, achieved through the solution of an ordinary differential equation. This method does not require any additional parameters and has been shown to effectively eliminate numerical oscillations and achieve high accuracy in a variety of test cases.

In a system consisting of a Bose-Einstein condensate and a single impurity, the quasimomentum of the condensate is significantly affected by the presence of the impurity. When the impurity is localized in a highly localized state after being coupled with the condensate, the final remnant decay of the condensate's oscillation occurs due to the interaction between the impurity and the condensate. Notably, the final remnant decay is influenced by the interaction between the two, which is crucial for observing this phenomenon. Furthermore, the final remnant decay can be induced by the presence of the impurity's internal structure, which affects the final remnant decay.

In the aftermath of a massive disaster, such as a hurricane, the delivery of essential supplies to isolated areas without functioning infrastructure poses a significant challenge. A novel framework has been proposed to tackle this problem, which incorporates both real-world and probabilistic approaches to optimize logistics under uncertainty conditions. The framework identifies the most critical aspects of the problem, such as adaptive planning and limited resource capacity, and proposes solutions for mitigating the risks associated with uncertain demand and supply. Through a multi-phase approach, the problem is broken down into sub-problems, and a combination of deterministic and stochastic optimization methods are applied to achieve optimal results, demonstrated through a case study of the 2020 Hurricane Hanna relief efforts in Texas.

The timing array's goal is to detect low-frequency signals from supermassive black hole pairs, utilizing a technique to enhance sensitivity by considering non-circular orbits. This study examines the effect of elliptical orbits on Pulsar Timing Array signals, specifically comparing the accuracy of two methods in computing these signals, given the complexity of computing elliptical solutions. One method uses an orbit with eccentricity set to the average of the black hole pair's eccentricities, while the other calculates the exact elliptical solution. By comparing the two approaches, we found that the average eccentricity method yields an error of about 10% in the waveform phase at second-and-a-half post-Newtonian precision, for black hole masses similar to those in the Pulsar Timing Array's target sample. Furthermore, we found that the exact elliptical solution method yields the same waveform phase for the same system, thus confirming its accuracy. This study also examines the computational efficiency of the average eccentricity method compared to the exact elliptical solution method.

In this research, we're examining a new dimension of global competition, focusing on global competitions where players' actions have global consequences. This includes strategy games where players make individual decisions that can impact the game's state, influencing other players in significant ways. Our work explores the global game framework, which allows us to analyze global competition by breaking it down into local components and their connections. We're particularly interested in how players' global knowledge and competition style affect the game's outcome, and our research shows that by watching the actions of other players, competitors gain valuable insights that can help them achieve better results. Our findings are based on a new algorithm that enables players to track the game's state and make informed decisions. We're also investigating the role of common knowledge among players in game dynamics and the impact of different decision-making styles on game outcomes. Our research has far-reaching implications for our understanding of global competition and decision-making processes.

A previously unexploited frequency range for detecting substances based on its spectral properties has been developed, enabling the precise measurement of on-chip samples at a frequency range of 750-1100 GHz. High-quality detectors were employed to accurately determine the spectral response of the developed system, resulting in detailed information about the absorption patterns of diverse substances such as water, ethanol, and glycerol. These patterns were found to be in close alignment with established models, further validating the effectiveness of this innovative technology. Moreover, this system demonstrated its capability to discern subtle differences in the absorption spectra of water-glycerol mixtures, thus underscoring its potential for applications such as detecting biomolecules and analyzing metabolic processes.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought to the forefront the importance of public health, revealing its critical links to economic, social, and economic well-being. As a response, computer science and artificial intelligence have become key strategies in preventing the spread of the virus and mitigating its impact. This research aims to develop an innovative approach to combatting COVID-19 by integrating various data-driven techniques and AI methods, ultimately leading to the development of an adaptable system that can be seamlessly integrated with existing processes in institutions, such as hospitals, schools, and airports.

In this research, we've developed a novel, multi-phase, fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model that incorporates a multiphase smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method with a massless, porous sphere model. This approach overcomes limitations of traditional methods by enabling the simulation of complex interactions between a Newtonian fluid and a deformable, porous red blood cell. To evaluate and refine our model, we performed a thorough sensitivity analysis on key parameters governing the interaction between the fluid and solid phases. Specifically, we varied initial conditions, the porosity of the solid phase, and the fluid-wetted surface tension coefficient. Our analysis revealed that the porosity significantly influences the fluid's resistance to the cell's drag force, while the fluid-wetted surface tension has a substantial effect on the overall interaction force. Furthermore, we observed that the initial conditions and the porosity can lead to either a splitting or merging of the fluid interphase when the interaction force is strong enough.

Nodal surfaces in momentum space, characterized by zero energy and zero group velocity, are present in specific models with symmetries. These models, protected by symmetries such as time reversal and inversion, exhibit robust nodal surfaces despite varying forms. The unique properties of these surfaces can be exploited for novel applications, including the creation of non-trivial optical beams without absorption. Recent experiments featuring photonic crystals, graphene-based devices, superlattices, and spin-orbit coupled systems have now made it possible to realize these concepts. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the underlying physical principles, specific model realizations, and experimental realizations of zero energy and zero group velocity nodal surfaces.

The HL-LHC computing model is shifting towards a Common Software Environment, utilizing the WLCG. Three software packages, Monte Carlo event generators, data processing frameworks, and framework-independent tools, were evaluated for selection. This document provides an overview of the event generators chosen in the initial selection, known as Stuey and Pythia8, their status, and plans. Key information includes input dataset, configuration options, development, testing, and deployment infrastructure, as well as plans for the future.

This paper utilizes Ramanujan invariants in the context of partial means, which are then utilized to identify specific partial means that share similar or equivalent values with established polynomials like the first Elliot polynomial, the second Elliot polynomial, and the first Van der Bunt polynomial, each defined over the rational numbers.

The outer galaxy's central region is a unique area where star formation is not influenced, according to previous CO emission research. Our study aimed to investigate the molecular gas distribution in this area using the Nobeyama Millimeter Radio Interferometer. We analyzed the distribution of 13CO and C18O emission lines at 106 pc radius, and found that 13CO emission lines were not detectable. Our analysis revealed a 1.9 K km/s velocity width for the 13CO emission lines, which is significantly narrower than typical galaxies. We also observed a 1.5 degree offset in the distribution of 12CO emission lines and a 0.5 degree offset in the distribution of 13CO emission lines. Our study suggests that the outer galaxy's disk is composed of dark, dense gas. Our analysis yielded a total mass of 1.0 x 10^7 M_sun for the outer galaxy's central region, which is a factor of two lower than the mass observed at 70 G0 3.

This paper examines the interconnected economic, social, and career outcomes resulting from a predetermined salary structure. Within a complex labor market, comprising multiple sectors with varying levels of correlation, each with unique and sector-based skill requirements, and labor markets that can be categorized as imperfectly competitive, we analyze how the system is affected by a set of predefined parameters. Key elements of the model include standardized skill sets, tiered career progression, and a focus on individual productivity rather than sector-specific conditions, all of which influence the system's dynamic behavior. Our research demonstrates that the introduction of a higher minimum wage initially leads to sustained employment within sectors characterized by high productivity, but may ultimately cause a significant decline in the market as a whole, culminating in an equilibrium where employment is eliminated in sectors with imperfectly competitive labor markets, and where a substantial portion of the workforce is unemployed.

The behavior of an active polar fluid in a two-dimensional setting is analyzed in the presence of random disorder. Using simulations that vary particle density, we examine the system's behavior across different regimes. At low density, the system exhibits a nematic phase that encompasses a wide range of densities when strong enough local nematic order develops. At low shear rates, the system displays a NAD (normal stress difference) that's parallel to the flow direction, which decreases as density increases, eventually disappearing in the turbulent regime. In this turbulent regime, the system also shows a non-mechanical stress that's perpendicular to the flow direction, which appears at low shear rates but persists in a strong shear regime, indicating a long-range correlation in the system's activity. This suggests that activity can induce a form of long-range order, even in an a priori disordered system.

Within a bag model framework, we investigated the semileptonic processes involving the transition of a doubly charmed baryon to another of the same type but with a changed spin state. Our research involved calculating the form factors and gauge-invariant currents, enabling us to determine form factor ratios and currents that could be compared to lattice data for validation. Notably, our study found that the ratios of form factors for the decay of $\Lambda_c^+$
to $\Lambda_c(2625)^-$ and $\Xi_c^+)$ to $\Xi_c(2810)^-$ matched closely with lattice data, particularly at zero momentum transfer. This agreement supports the applicability of the bag model in describing the transition of a doubly charmed baryon to another of the same type but with a changed spin state.

This study introduces a new task of embedding physical locations based on interactive body movements, known as a scene understanding task. To investigate this problem, a new benchmark is created from the VirtualHome Environment, consisting of challenging scenarios with complex locations and varying levels of difficulty. To address this challenge, a novel approach is proposed that incorporates body part queries and spatial referencing for improved localization, resulting in higher accuracy. Additionally, the task and proposed methods are evaluated using a unique combination of human and machine models, with the machine models trained on virtual data and fine-tuned using human-in-the-loop data.

This research introduces an automated frequency band selection technique called Band Importance Factor (BIF) for analyzing rotating machinery vibrations. The BIF method is capable of generating a single importance score for pre-defined frequency ranges. It does this by analyzing the distribution of vibration frequencies within each range relative to a machine's balance frequency. The BIF method is then applied to a range of real-world vibration data from industrial rotating machinery, specifically after initial processing to remove baseline vibrations and to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio. The results from the BIF method are then compared with those from existing techniques, such as the Hilbert Envelope and Hilbert Transform, as well as with manual analysis by operators.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of the superconducting states of CaTSi3 compounds with T = Ir and Pt using muon spectroscopy. Our results indicate that both compounds exhibit non-unitary behavior in their superconducting states, as evidenced by temperature-dependent relaxation rates in zero field. Additionally, we observed a uniform and high-frequency spin phase in a transverse field of 6.5 mT for CaTiSi3 at temperatures below 8.5K, suggesting a noncentrosymmetric multicomponent order parameter. Conversely, this type of behavior was not observed in CaPtSi3 at temperatures below 5.5K, with its muon spin rotation signal displaying a uniform phase at all temperatures. Our findings imply that CaPtSi3 exhibits a unitary state of superconductivity, with an isotropic and single-component order parameter.

We're investigating sparse grid methods as a means to overcome the 'curse of dimensionality' when solving Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations, specifically in feedback control and regulation problems with finite horizon and infinite time horizon. This study aims to bridge the existing literature on sparse grid methods for state and value function propagation simultaneously. We're applying this method to real-world systems like the ACDC cart, a inverted pendulum, and a spacecraft. Our findings indicate that sparse grid methods are efficient, reliable, and capable of bypassing the 'curse of dimensionality' when applied to systems with bounded states, providing high-precision results, and outperforming existing sparse grid methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Recent breakthroughs in quantum machine learning have demonstrated the potential
of quantum computers in solving various machine learning tasks more efficiently.
This study focuses on the quantum evaluation classification task, where we investigate
the feasibility of using quantum computers to perform tasks analogous to classical
neural network classification methods. We examine this task using binary (qubit)
quantum systems and generalized binary (qudit) systems, and we propose innovative
methods for processing binary and qudit data. Our findings show that, in some
cases, using binary systems can achieve superior performance and training speed
over qudits, whereas in other instances, qudits can yield improved results. Our
study further reveals that qudits may be more effective than binary systems for
certain tasks, and we identify specific scenarios where qudits or binary systems
can produce superior outcomes.

The integration of renewable energy and advanced power electronics in the energy system creates a complex, dynamic environment. The rapid growth of renewable energy sources, combined with an increase in the dynamic elements of power systems, necessitates a shift from static to dynamic modeling and control. The intricate relationships between multiple energy domains, including the power system, heat networks, and chemical processes, further complicate the already dynamic energy system. This study addresses the challenges of managing such complex systems by providing a framework that highlights the synergies between dynamic control and multi-objective optimization. The study demonstrates how advanced dynamic control can facilitate the decarbonization of energy systems by showcasing its application in a numerical example based on a multi-energy system.

The 2D filtration process is a fundamental concept, applicable to a wide range of processes, such as biological, chemical, mechanical, etc. This process is characterized by the gradual refinement of structures, governed by the principle that smaller elements combine to form larger ones. In this context, we have applied the 2D filtration principle to machine intelligence, treating algorithms as filters. This application has revealed interesting connections between algorithmic complexity and the 2D filtration model, particularly in how different algorithms, such as backpropagation and gradient descent, reflect the process of filtering information.

Researchers employed a unique 1H magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique to closely examine the heat distribution within a packed gas-solid bed at different atmospheric conditions. The study focused on a bed with particles measuring 1.5 mm in diameter and containing a mixture of helium and nitrogen gases at 40°C temperature, spanning from low to high pressure levels. The MRI analysis revealed that the fluid phase's heat distribution is primarily controlled by both gas and particle thermal conduction, with the thermal conduction coefficient varying between 0.3 and 0.5. The researchers also found that the fluid-particle heat transfer mechanism can be described by a constant heat transfer coefficient that ranges between 1.5 and 2.5 times higher than the gas convective heat transfer capacity. The MRI results further showed that increasing pressure enhances the heat transfer between the gas and particle phases.

In superconductors, introducing a degree of unpredictability to the interconnections between electrons can trigger a resurgence of superconductivity under specific temperature conditions. Our theoretical analysis indicates that a thermal change in the system's unpredictability leads to a specific pattern of superconductivity changes, demonstrating a reentrance mechanism. This reentrance is characterized by superconductivity emerging at high temperatures, peaking in the middle range before disappearing at low temperatures. This complex behavior is distinguishable in the temperature dependence of the superconducting critical temperature and the area under its hysteresis curve. We have successfully applied this model to UTe$_2$, a compound exhibiting this reentrant superconductivity.

In recent years, UWB technology has been gaining traction for indoor positioning due to its ability to provide accurate sub-centimeter location tracking and high sub-millisecond timing precision. UWB's versatility makes it a promising technology for a variety of applications, such as positioning and communication, due to its wide range of available radio configurations. To optimize UWB signal transmission, the transmitter and receiver must agree on a common configuration. In real-time interactive settings, fine-tuning this configuration in real-time can lead to improved system performance, which is particularly beneficial in environments where the radio propagation characteristics change frequently. In this study, we present a novel deep reinforcement learning method for dynamically adjusting UWB radio configurations in real-time based on channel state information. Our simulator models the UWB signal transmission in real-world scenarios, simulating various transmitter-receiver configurations and complex channel conditions. Our simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in a time-varying environment, showcasing its potential to achieve higher throughput compared to traditional UWB configurations.

We investigate the $k$-median clustering problem in a metric space, which includes two key metrics: the Fr\'echet distance and the Hausdorff distance, both defined on a set of finite points in $\mathbb{R}^2$. We demonstrate that the difference in the cost between the optimal and a near-optimal solution remains relatively small when the number of points in the set is limited. Specifically, we establish upper bounds for the cost difference in terms of the number of points, the number of clusters ($k$), and the distance metric. These bounds are then shown to be tight and include both upper and lower bounds. Notably, the cost difference is shown to be independent of the size of the underlying space, which is a key advantage of our approach.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning presents a challenging problem due to its sequential decision-making nature and information exchange limitations, necessitating a general algorithm for this complex task. We introduce a reinforcement learning-based method that modifies established algorithms to accommodate multiple agents with distinct policies, yielding a workable solution. Building on these foundations, we developed MAD3QN, an innovative algorithm that optimizes a collective reward function through two types of averaging. MAD3QN was successfully applied to the Multi-Agent DQN, an instance of a primal-dual gradient algorithm, and also extended to the multi-agent context of the Double Q-Value Algorithm, a gradient-free method. We demonstrated MAD3QN's high performance in both the Multi-Agent Navigation and the Cooperative Gridworld domains, achieving superior results compared to existing algorithms.

We establish a coalgebraic framework for verifying the correct implementation of arithmetic $\mu$-programs, and subsequently develop a theorem prover based on this framework. Notably, our method can validate specifications for both loop-free programs and those with loops of any complexity, by interpreting loops as coalgebras. This results in a function that determines whether a program meets its specified requirements. Moreover, our approach allows for the creation of a executable verification tool, known as MuApro, that runs directly from specifications. The executable verification tool correctly identifies whether a given program satisfies its specified loop condition.

In this work, we explore the concept of Isogeometric Analysis for solving partial differential equations, specifically focusing on the potential to leverage the sparsity of discrete solutions for guiding the construction of their initial conditions. By using Isogeometric B-splines, our discretization methods result in solvers that can exploit sparse matrices, but we also find that the initial conditions themselves often have sparse forms that go unexploited with this approach. To address this issue, we utilize the reduced-rank tensor techniques to efficiently compress and reconstruct sparse initial conditions for PDEs in a non-intrusive manner. Our approach involves three main steps: first, we use Isogeometric Galerkin methods to numerically compute the linear dependence between the solution's modes; second, we employ the CPWL approximation to describe the dependence structure of the solution in a non-parametric way; and third, we use the reduced-rank tensor techniques to provide an interpretable and efficient approximation of the solution's dependence structure. Our numerical experiments on the Burgers' equation and the shallow water equations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of both the quality of the approximation and the computational efficiency of the solution method.

The rapid growth in smart devices is generating massive wireless data that needs to be efficiently transmitted. But current wireless systems are limited by congested channels and a shortage of resources, making it hard to meet increasing demand. To overcome this, our research suggests using predictive sensing methods that can anticipate and predict the location and usage of limited resources, like air-conditioned facilities, without needing to directly measure them. This approach leverages a model of facility location and usage, allowing us to estimate the status of AC drives in buildings without having to directly sense them. This can be done by learning the correlation between AC drive position and power consumption from a small number of sensors. Once the positions are determined, the power consumption can be estimated based on the specific facility and time of day. This allows for the creation of a dense map of wireless access points in a given area, and a comparison with real-world measurements shows that this method can accurately predict the power consumption of AC drives with an error rate of less than 5%.

This study aims to develop representations of the generalized linear group $\mathrm{GL}_n(Q,\sigma)$, where $Q$ is a ring comprised of truncated power series over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, with $q$ being an odd prime power. The group $\mathrm{GL}_n(Q,\sigma)$ contains the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}_n(Q,\sigma)$ as a normal subgroup since $Q$ is $\sigma$-invariant. The representation sought after is a Weil type representation, which means it must be non-trivial, absolutely irreducible, and unique (up to isomorphism). To achieve this, we employ the theory of $L$-rings and develop a specific Weil $L$-ring for the given group. We establish that the center of the Hecke algebra associated with the representation is a polynomial ring over the center of $Q$. Additionally, we identify the unramified part of the representation by establishing a p-completion of the group as a finite index subgroup.

The advancement of video editing technology has allowed for the development of sophisticated methods to manipulate video content, giving rise to an emerging field of research on creating realistic and engaging videos. This article provides an in-depth review of the current techniques for creating engaging videos, categorized into two main areas: techniques that use implicit methods to enhance visual and auditory aspects and those that use explicit models to create engaging and interactive content. Additionally, future research directions and challenges in this field are discussed.

This paper introduces a method for compressing the coherent states of motion in ion traps by manipulating the ion trap design. The approach involves optimizing the shape of the confinement potential to minimize the orthogonal components of the ion's motion. By doing so, the method enables the creation of a quadrupole trap that can be used to produce compressed coherent states of motion, similar to those achieved in optical lattices. Additionally, the method is shown to be applicable to hexapole traps, where it can be used to confine multiple sets of quasi-lattices. The study's findings are demonstrated using numerical simulations for both types of traps.

The computational modeling of life sciences relies heavily on simulating complex biological systems, but this process often involves significant computational costs and numerous model parameters. To overcome these challenges, machine learning techniques can be employed to automate the simulation process. In this research, a novel framework was developed to efficiently simulate large-scale neural networks by integrating reinforcement learning, meta-learning, and neural networks. Our proposed algorithm, MetaRLNN, utilizes meta-learning to optimize reinforcement learning agents and neural networks to simulate neural spiking activity. The results of our experiments, conducted on high-performance computing systems, demonstrate the efficient simulation of a large neural network, with our approach outperforming traditional methods in terms of simulation speed.

We introduce a novel dataset, CINS, for the " Concealed Object Segmentation " problem where objects are hidden within complex backgrounds. This requires not only identifying the masked areas but also generating the original shape of the masked object. To address the difficulty of obtaining labeled data, we created a large, unbalanced, self-supervised, in-the-wild dataset, CINS-IWS, using an innovative method. The dataset is then used to develop a two-stage segmentation approach, which first locates the masked objects and then produces the missing regions. The performance of the model is evaluated using multiple metrics, including novel metrics for the segmentation of masked areas. We also examine the impact of pre-training on the model's performance and provide a baseline for future research.

This paper explores the effects of violating the second law of Lorentz invariance on the phenomenon of high-temperature superconductivity. A modified London-Frankel equation is employed to derive the critical magnetic field required for superconducting transition in a two-layered material. In this analysis, we consider a two-dimensional, anisotropic superconductor with a layer perpendicular to the Lorentz or time axis.

As AI's presence in critical systems grows, ensuring its reliability becomes increasingly vital.  Our method allows end-users of AI systems to report issues, providing valuable information that is used to create a test suite.  Our tool, called Verify, automatically generates tests based on these reports, enabling the validation of reported problems and the identification of additional edge cases.  Our system has been successfully implemented in various applications and gathered thousands of reports from thousands of users.  In a study, we found that users' reports are highly accurate and effective in exposing both reported problems and newly discovered issues.  Our method has significant potential to improve AI's reliability by making it accessible to a broader audience and reducing the need for extensive testing by professionals.

Object detection in images relies on accurate localization and identification of objects. However, current approaches often sacrifice one aspect for the other: proposals either provide high localization accuracy but are limited in their identification capabilities, or they offer robust identification but are less precise in localization. To overcome this trade-off, a new stochastic decision-making technique is introduced in this work. It's called Stochastic Decision Routing for object detection (RDet) and involves training multiple networks with different architectures, each suited to a specific range of object sizes. During processing, the proposed method dynamically decides which network to use, based on the size of the object in question. To ensure seamless transitions between networks, a specialized training schedule is employed. Our method has been tested on the MS-COCO benchmark and produced significant results: an absolute improvement of 1.8% in mAP when processing the full image and 0.6% when processing 800x600 pixels.

ZeroGrad is an easy-to-implement optimization technique that significantly reduces overfitting when using FGSM adversarial training. When using this method, model parameters are updated only when the gradient magnitudes are below a specified threshold during training, and left unchanged otherwise. This description may seem similar to "noise early stopping" and dynamic threshold techniques, but it differs in setting static thresholds for each layer. We found that incorporating ZeroGrad in FGSM adversarial training can effectively prevent catastrophic overfitting and maintain the method's robustness. This technique can be applied not only to the standard FGSM adversarial training but also to other variants that use different types of losses, including the loss within the inner loop, the loss within the outer loop, and the combined loss.

Recent research on primordial black holes has been reevaluated based on the accurate analysis of their gravitational wave properties. A previously used approximation, the Thakurta metric, has been found to be insufficient for high-energy wave descriptions. A more suitable alternative, the bi-conic metric, provides a more precise model. However, it is discovered that the bi-conic metric and Thakurta metric exhibit identical low-frequency behaviors, meaning that the existing LIGO-Virgo data constraints on PBHs remain unaltered despite the change in metric description.

In recent years, several hybrid optimization algorithms have been proposed to improve the efficiency of single objective optimization tasks. These algorithms combine the strengths of different search methods, leading to a potential for synergistic interactions that enhance their performance. Traditional hybrid algorithms involve periodic changes to the search method at predetermined points in the optimization process. This study investigates the effect of continuously adjusting the search method as the solution evolves, with a focus on a class of improved variants of the Non-Correlated Simulated Annealing (NSA) algorithm. The results of experiments conducted on diverse test suites, including both standard and hybrid problems, reveal that fine-tuning the search method in real-time can result in significant performance enhancements, particularly when the search process is slowed down.

Bounded-depth Frege Holes can be solved efficiently in fully homomorphic encryption systems, but this does not allow for the resolution of DeMorgan's Theorem problems due to the lack of homomorphic properties in the mod $2^{k}$ operator. In an attempt to address this limitation, researchers have introduced a new fully homomorphic encryption scheme, dubbed Bootstrappable Homomorphic Encryption System (BHT). A key challenge in BHT implementation is the scarcity of efficient methods for solving Holes in this context. To address this problem, we have developed a new protocol, referred to as Binary Tree Splitting (BTS), which enables the resolution of Holes in BHT efficiently. In an ideal binary tree structure for Holes, BTS uses an efficient decomposition method, resulting in an average of $\log n$ decompositions, and achieves an efficient bootstrapping process. In an ideal binary tree structure for depth-$\Delta$ Holes, BTS uses an efficient decomposition, resulting in an average of $\log^{(\Delta+1)} n$ decompositions, and achieves an efficient bootstrapping process.

This paper delves into several types of solvable random matrix ensembles derived from stochastic processes, including the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, the harmonic oscillator process, the Ornstein-Richardson process, the Brownian motion with a confining potential, the Bessel bridge, the Ornstein-Richardson-Uhlenbeck process, the geometric Brownian motion with a confining potential, the Ornstein-Richardson-Uhlencky process, the squared Bessel process, the Brownian motion with a confining potential, the Lamé process, the geometric Brownian motion with a confining potential, the confining harmonic oscillator, the Lamé-Heun equation, the confining hyperbolic Brownian motion, the Lamé Bessel process, the confining hyperbolic Brownian motion with time-dependent coefficients, the Lamé-Heun equation with variable coefficients, and the confining Brownian motion with time-dependent coefficients. The study covers the stochastic characteristics, including mean, variance, and higher-order moments, as well as the cumulant generating function, distributional limits, and large deviations for these processes. Additionally, it explores the first-passage time distributions and their Laplace transforms, providing an in-depth comparison with the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in various aspects.

Our research experimentally examines the connection dynamics between three-leg and four-leg states in a quantum system consisting of two particles with unique spin properties. This study found that the connection between specific states in the three-party system is directly proportional to the strength of its magnetic field and lasts longer when the field is stronger. It is also observed that the connection between the three-party system is directly proportional to the strength of its internal connections and the strength of its magnetic field, and this is also true for the connection between the three-party system and an external particle. However, the connection between the three-party system is directly proportional to the strength of its internal connections, but the connection between the system and an external particle is only true if the particle is connected to the system.

In the context of a local hidden variables theory, we explore the nature of total probability distributions. Our analysis indicates that the locality condition has a dual consequence: the ability to break down a Bell correlation into separate, monogamous correlations and the existence of a maximum interferometric efficiency for such separable rates. These findings are demonstrated using the mathematical framework of simple probability distributions and the example of a binary singlet state experiment, where two parties engage in a task that violates the Bell's no-go theorem for blind quantum processing.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a versatile video generation tool, capable of producing high-quality videos at 256x256 resolution. Unlike existing GAN-based methods, StyleGAN-V operates in real-time, allowing for seamless video editing and continuous control. This is achieved through a unique combination of a low-dimensional latent space and a non-intrusive sampling technique, both of which are learned simultaneously during training. Notably, StyleGAN-V is trained using only a single video dataset, without the need for additional 2D/3D video or audio datasets. We demonstrate the efficacy of StyleGAN-V by showcasing its ability to generate long, smooth and high-quality videos across multiple video domains.

We examine the differences in degrees associated with the global lifts of symmetric weakly holomorphic modular forms from their image under the eta correspondence map to their original version. The calculated degree discrepancies will be expressed in terms of generator series of the form $\prod_{i=1}^4 \eta(i)^{s_i}$.

A novel deep learning strategy has been developed to improve the accuracy of dose estimation from luminescence readings by over 80%. This technique leverages the ability of neural networks to analyze complex data and create more accurate models, surpassing previous methods that relied on statistical relationships between glow curves. By training the model on data with noise and signal disturbances, it becomes highly adaptable and resilient. When applied to low-quality readings with signal-to-noise ratios as low as 10^-6, the approach yields accurate results with minimal error. Notably, the approach eliminates the need for readings to regain their initial brightness, a limitation that previously required storing doses for an extended period. By processing data in a matter of seconds, the approach enables near-instant dose estimation, making it possible to rapidly evaluate doses and apply them to various applications, including patient dosimetry.

This paper explores the existence and non-existence of weak solutions for a particular type of nonlinear singular parabolic equations in a complete manifold. The equations involve a singular term that is defined by $\mathcal{Q}_i(x,t)=\frac{f(x, \nabla u(x), t)}{[a(x)]^\gamma \max\{\Vert f(x, \nabla u(x), t)\Vert_{L^{\frac{1}{p}}_x}, 1\}}$. We consider this type of equation within the context of Sobolev spaces with variable exponents $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ and Orlicz space exponents $r(x)$ and $s(x)$. We analyze the properties of the nonlinear function $f(x, \alpha)$ and the weight function $a(x)$ and show that existence and non-existence of weak solutions can be influenced by the regularity of $f(x, \alpha)$ and the behavior of the weight function $a(x)$, specifically whether it belongs to the Muckenhoupt-Ackermann class $w_{p(x), p'(x), \beta(x)}(\R^n)$ or not.

Accurate simulation of cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) cone angles and X-ray spectrum is crucial for CBCT dose calculation and development. The Fastcat simulation software efficiently models these characteristics, enabling rapid and precise calculations. This study verified the accuracy of Fastcat-generated data for CBCT settings of 80 kV, 150 kV, and 220 kV along with several cone angles. The Fastcat data were validated against experimental measurements obtained from a Varian CBCT scanner. The results showed that Fastcat's simulated spectra closely matched actual measurements with differences less than 4%. Additionally, the Fastcat-generated dose profiles were consistent with experimental measurements within 5%. The discrepancies observed were primarily due to differences in CBCT collimation angle and source to focus distance, as well as the scattering effect in the CBCT head. These findings confirm that Fastcat can accurately simulate CBCT settings, facilitating rapid and precise calculations for CBCT dosimetry and development.

The increasing reliance on machine learning models in critical decision-making processes has highlighted the need to understand their decision-making processes.  While post-hoc techniques, such as model-agnostic explanations, have been developed to provide insights into these processes, their effectiveness is often hindered by the inherent limitations of the underlying models.  A notable example of this is the LIME technique, which is susceptible to certain limitations.  To address this, we introduce a novel technique, S-LIME, that mitigates these limitations by incorporating a stability metric to identify relevant features, thus enhancing the reliability of its explanations.  Our experiments, which involved applying S-LIME and LIME to a range of datasets, demonstrate its superiority in providing more accurate and stable explanations, particularly in situations where models are prone to overfitting.  Furthermore, S-LIME's applicability extends to models that are sensitive to feature scaling, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying data.  Overall, our results confirm the efficacy of S-LIME in generating more reliable explanations, which hold greater potential for practical applications.

Machine learning models are often viewed as black boxes, strictly taking in inputs and providing outputs without offering any insight into their decision-making process. Despite this limitation, certain machine learning models like those that incorporate rule-based reasoning can theoretically justify their results. This study proposes a classification method that draws from the principles of Bayesian analysis to correct classification errors by leveraging feedback from the model's justification, which is defined as the relative weight of supporting and opposing evidence for a specific classification outcome. This approach is demonstrated through a simulated experiment involving a decision tree classifier on two data sets. The results indicate that the classifier's correction rate surpasses 50% in certain cases when errors are made. This framework has the potential to be expanded to other classifiers that can provide justification, which is seen as a promising area for further research.

Recent studies on TbInO$_3$ have sparked interest in its potential as a spin-liquid crystal due to its unique characteristics, including a strong Tb$^{3+}$ crystal field and unusual magnetic susceptibility patterns. However, the underlying causes of these features remain unclear. Our comprehensive theoretical analysis of TbInO$_3$ reveals that the key to its properties lies in the single-ion anisotropy of the Tb$^{3+}$ ion. We found that the unusual susceptibility patterns are caused by the interaction between the crystal-field excitations and the lattice vibrations. Furthermore, the magnetic excitations exhibit complex vibronic patterns characterized by the interplay between the spin-rotation symmetry and the parity symmetry. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our theoretical approach in accurately predicting the experimental results, and we believe it will serve as a valuable framework for understanding the properties of other rare-earth compounds.

We demonstrate the existence of smooth solutions to the modified mean curvature flow, which are uniformly convex and have an appropriately regulated initial surface. Furthermore, this solution remains convex and maintains regularity over an extended period. In this context, the modified mean curvature is derived from the n-th power of the second-order mean curvature. This result surpasses a prior finding by Choe, which established the existence of a uniformly convex, smooth solution, however, this solution was found to be weak, meaning it had a single 30-degree angle singularity after a brief time interval.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to the remarkable ability of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to be trained using vast amounts of labeled image data. However, the process faces significant hurdles when dealing with real-world signals, such as time-series medical data, which are often scarce and difficult to label. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a pioneering approach to training CNNs with complex electromagnetic signals in the frequency domain, bypassing the need for expensive time-domain signal acquisition. By utilizing a fully connected architecture, the method demonstrates impressive results, achieving a remarkable accuracy of over 99.99% in classifying electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, with only a minimal amount of available data.

Recent studies have shown that utilizing deep neural networks for image grouping is both efficient and effective, particularly when compared to traditional approaches. However, deep models are susceptible to image noise and variations, which can compromise their performance when processing images with minor distortions. To address this limitation, deep models are often trained on noisy images. Consequently, the models are designed to handle noise rather than accurately representing the image content. To overcome these drawbacks, this research proposes the Deep Clutter Ensemble (DeepCluE) framework, which aims to enhance image grouping capabilities by utilizing multiple deep models to produce a range of image grouping scores. By combining these scores using a ranking-based aggregation method, DeepCluE accurately determines the most suitable grouping solution for a given image. Experimental results demonstrate that DeepCluE achieves superior image grouping performance when compared to the current state-of-the-art method.

The concept of risk recognition, encompassing the process of identifying potential losses and assessing their likelihood and severity in a specific organizational context, serves as a critical link between risk management and event occurrence. Risk management involves a range of mitigation strategies, including training and preparedness plans, emergency response procedures, and measures to decrease exposure to hazards. External factors, such as social and economic conditions, can significantly influence an organization's risk profile, particularly in the face of global events like epidemics, terrorist attacks, and environmental disasters. This research presents a novel method for creating a knowledge graph based on open-source knowledge that simulates an organization's risk management system. This framework enables the extraction of potential risks through the analysis of news articles, which are then matched against the organization's risk graph. Researchers tested this system by developing a risk graph for a university and applied it to a comparative analysis of global risks mentioned in The New York Times articles from 2020.

Data categorization, a fundamental process in data analysis, relies heavily on categorization. This study introduces a novel method for categorizing data using topological characteristics within density-based clusters, allowing for an unbiased comparison of clustering outcomes. By comparing pre- and post-clustering data, it is possible to identify and assess the effectiveness of various categorization methods. Our approach utilizes TDA to systematically analyze these comparisons, revealing the strengths and limitations of different clustering techniques.

We introduce a language that captures contrasimilarity domains, a concept previously defined in relation to concurrent systems and quantitative reframings of transition systems. Similarities with game description languages are noted, drawing links to existing formalisms due to the domain's connection to omega-chain complete duality, implying the existence of dual well-structured transition systems. This also allows for a quantitative generalisation of the Hennessy-Milner theorem to contrasimilarity, building upon prior work in the well-structured literature.

This paper provides a detailed introduction to the generalized string 2-group constructed from the string Lie algebra associated with a given Lie algebra, with a focus on Lie algebras that are relevant in the context of string theory and related areas. A primary objective of this work is to highlight the importance of the string 2-group in its role in defining the automorphism symmetries of string Lie algebras and cohomology structures that are invariant under string 2-group actions. The concept of the string 2-group has implications for the development of string Lie 2-algebras, as well as the potential for the generation of string theory 2-algebras that are invariant under certain conditions. The existing literature has been reviewed, with a focus on the connections between string 2-algebras, string Lie 2-algebras, and string 2-groups, as well as the relationship between the string 2-group and the higher analogs of string theory concepts. The development of a string 2-group based on the string Lie algebra of the Poincaré algebra has also been explored, with a focus on the implications for the associated string theory 2-algebra.
