The emergence of blockchain technology has led to a proliferation of decentralized applications, which utilize smart contracts to automate processes. However, the current state of these contracts is plagued by several limitations, which hinder their efficiency and usability. To address these issues, this study presents a novel approach, which transforms smart contracts into functions within a decentralized computing protocol. This protocol, named Marvel DC, leverages a blockchain-based interface for node operation and a custom function call method to create a seamless and interoperable ecosystem. As a result, the proposed solution enables the execution of decentralized applications with unparalleled flexibility, compatibility, and reliability.

A new perceptual quality prediction model has been developed to improve the evaluation of 3D point cloud compression. This decreased reference perceptual quality model (DRPQ) takes into account distortion in the base layer and applies a weighted filter to the base layer and an incremental layer, resulting in a refined estimate of the compressed output layer. The DRPQ has been tested and found to more accurately reflect the visually significant information in the compressed data, resulting in lower prediction errors than previous models. As a result, the DRPQ has been adopted by the MPEG ad hoc group for use in evaluating 3D data after base-layer compression. Additionally, the DRPQ has been applied to the rate control of 3D plug-in point cloud compression tools, resulting in improved compression performance at various bitrates.

In holography, researchers have employed a method to map the QCD phase diagram through the lens of Borel $N$-point conformal blocks. This approach reveals the non-perturbative structure of deconfinement transition in chiral and large volume phases, and the conformal block effectively models the Taylor series expansion of the Polyakov loop. The method also predicts that the chiral dimension at the phase transition is directly proportional to the large N expansion and the inverse square root of the system volume. The theory is applied to a non-perturbative model for QCD thermodynamics and phase transitions. The results obtained from this holographic model align qualitatively with the Lattice QCD data. The method is further extended to model the Polykov Loop correlator as the vacuum expectation value of a massive scalar field in a de Sitter background, subjected to a hard wall boundary condition. The results obtained from this model also show qualitative agreement with the Lattice QCD phase diagram.

Knee joint abnormalities can be challenging to diagnose with MRI, often requiring multiple scans and a long time. To improve knee anomaly classification using MRI, we present a novel method combining the strengths of 3D image slicing and self-supervised learning. Our approach, SB-SSL, utilizes a transformer-based model to process 2D slices from MRI scans, with a custom loss function that encourages the network to capture meaningful features. In our study, SB-SSL demonstrated superior performance compared to a baseline model on a knee MRI dataset.

Creating new typesfaces with a limited number of examples is a challenging problem in few-shot font generation. Existing approaches typically create new typesfaces by taking the average of the input types or using all the examples simultaneously, which can result in low-quality or non-existent typefaces when the input examples vary significantly or are limited in number. Our research focuses on developing a method to generate high-quality, novel typefaces from a small collection of examples, even when the input types are diverse. The key to this approach lies in defining local styles at the level of individual characters and representing them as spatial patterns defined by a set of control points. We propose a novel technique for learning local styles by analyzing the input types and use this knowledge to create new typefaces that accurately capture the nuances of the input examples, as well as their overall aesthetic. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in creating new typefaces from a small number of examples, even in high-contrast and low-data settings.

In equilibrium, liquids with broken time-reversal symmetry exhibit non-trivial properties. Our research reveals that such liquids can also possess an extra symmetry beyond chirality. We discovered that the equilibrium state of a chiral nematic liquid in a cell can be influenced by external stimuli, despite the lack of net torque. Our analysis focuses on the torsional mode, which allows for the manipulation of nematic director orientation within the cell. Our findings demonstrate that the torsional mode can induce unique, non-trivial effects on the chiral nematic flow and stress tensor, resulting in the emergence of novel viscoelastic properties. Furthermore, we observed that the torsional mode can also induce a non-trivial response to the chiral coupling, leading to the generation of a non-zero stress tensor with a unique structure. Our study provides insights into the complex behavior of chiral nematic liquids and offers potential applications in controlling flow and stress responses through precise control of torsional stimuli.

The widespread use of adaptive video streaming has been hindered by inconsistent quality of experience (QoE). Current methods rely on standardized QoE models based on limited data, leading to suboptimal video quality and low user satisfaction. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach for improving QoE through a digital twin-based system. This system uses a digital replica of the network and a sophisticated algorithm to optimize video quality in real-time by taking into account network conditions, video content, and user preferences. The effectiveness of this method has been confirmed through simulations, which showed a significant improvement in video quality, with a 12.5% increase in visual quality and a 5% decrease in user dissatisfaction compared to traditional adaptive video streaming.

The KM3NeT neutrino detector concept employs thousands of photomultiplier readouts per ton, resulting in an exceptionally low threshold for detecting neutrinos and resolving the direction of incoming light. Its proven technology, particularly the long-distance optical fibers, enables a larger volume than its predecessor, IMB-DUSEL reference design, had initially, by utilizing a double cascade process to identify optical signals. This innovative strategy circumvents the need for high-cost components like wave-length shifting plates and quartz-fiber light guides while maintaining its detection capabilities, as demonstrated by the successful application of this approach in a detector located at the ArgoNeutel site at the sea floor, utilizing three different types of sensors.

The study focuses on the periodic nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation with the addition of space-time rough noise in its dissipative inhomogeneous form. We demonstrate that even when the noise is not small, the resulting stochastic equation maintains a unique inhomogeneous dissipative solution, thereby resolving a previous issue regarding the convergence of semigroups with the introduction of significant noise. We achieve this through a combination of methods, including the application of the parabolic Anderson model in 2D, the direct investigation of the stochastic monochromatic model, and the application of the Ito formula with variable coefficients.

This study presents an innovative joint encoding and coordination strategy to ensure
reliable communication on multiple parallel wireless connections within a specific
delay constraint, aiming to maximize the overall data transmission rate. Two diverse
communication scenarios are examined: the first involves a single source transmitting
to multiple receivers through separate channels, whereas the second involves multiple
sources transmitting data to a single receiver. To tackle these challenges, we develop
two dynamic programming-based algorithms that solve the joint encoding and
coordination problem exactly. Theoretical evidence supports the effectiveness of our
methods, and numerical simulations confirm their ability to maximize transmission
efficiency in various scenarios.

The origins of the Sgr A East supernova remnant remain a topic of ongoing research. Recent studies have proposed various theories, including a dual explosion model, where the explosion that created the central X-ray source occurred before or simultaneously with the main supernova that generated the visible and radio emissions observed today. In this study, we investigate the possibility that the X-ray source formed during the primary supernova, by re-examining the timing and spatial constraints of the explosion using the dual explosion model, and considering the dynamics of the remnant remnant in the Milky Way's central star cluster. By analyzing the age and size of the remnant and its expansion speed, we can determine whether the X-ray source and main supernova, which created the remnant, occurred at the same or different times, and whether the main supernova occurred in a dense environment. Our results suggest that the X-ray source and main supernova likely occurred at the same time, and the main supernova occurred in a relatively low-density environment, which is consistent with the dense explosion theory.

We suggest a solution to the long-standing problem of lepton flavor universality violation in B transitions, focusing on the rare decay of B to K* gamma. Our proposed solution incorporates two key new physics elements: first, a vector current affecting the quark level; and second, a left-handed current that can be interpreted as a top quark involvement in the decay process, offering a potential resolution to the similar lepton flavor universality anomaly observed in the B to K mu plus plus decay. We explore the underlying group structure and the corresponding symmetry that governs the effective Hamiltonian for this decay process. Our calculations indicate that the resulting lepton flavor universality violation is within the detection limits of the LHCb detector, and future experiments may provide insight into the nature of the involved Yukawa couplings.

This research paper outlines our approach to the 2021 DISRPT shared task, specifically focusing on three key aspects of text analysis: identifying discourse segments, classifying each segment, and pinpointing key relationships between them. To tackle these challenges, we leveraged a range of techniques, including cutting-edge neural networks and sophisticated traditional methods. Our results from the shared task, which evaluated the performance of various models on multiple publicly accessible datasets, reveal that our approach is highly effective in both overall segment identification and relationship classification tasks.

The sharing of physical infrastructure is a vital component of the future network and communication technology in 6G and beyond. However, it faces significant challenges due to a trust gap between service providers and the entities sharing resources. To address this issue, the concept of 'trustworthiness' is introduced as a key factor in establishing reliable and clear infrastructure sharing. To increase trust among parties, the proposed BEAT framework leverages a blockchain and artificial intelligence-driven approach. The framework's core components are 6G/Beyond-Small Cells, Virtual Shared Resources, and the Security Infrastructure Sharing Blockchain Network (SISBN). The SISBN serves as the backbone of the BEAT framework, providing a secure and efficient way to share physical infrastructure. To ensure the scalability of the infrastructure sharing network, the SISBN employs a Delegated Proof of Stake (DPOS) consensus mechanism, ensuring that the network's operations are efficient and sustainable. The proposed framework's security analysis reveals that the SISBN achieves a high level of confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. The experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the SISBN, yielding an average consensus time of 1.5 seconds. The proposed framework's performance is also evaluated using the 3GPP TR 22.891 model, showing that the SISBN can handle a large number of users, even in scenarios with high network latency and network congestion.

This work introduces a nonlinear mathematical framework to investigate the Okubo-Weiss standards in two-dimensional fluid and magnetofluid flows. The approach involves deriving a two-dimensional, nonlinear fluid flow model around a rotating cylinder and then converting it into a dimensionless form, which provides insight into the dynamics of vortices and wave-like disturbances. By analyzing this model, the conditions under which the Okubo-Weiss criteria predict the presence of singularity or stable vortex motion are identified. The research also examines the influence of rotation and magnetic field intensity on these criteria.

Lee-Wick theories incorporate negative energy particles linked with their positive energy counterparts, resulting in unique thermodynamic properties. These theories alter both the quantum and classical dynamics, specifically introducing a different Lagrangian density that includes a reversible term with a negative Lagrangian density. This paper investigates the effects of Lee-Wick theories on the early universe, focusing on the pre-big bang phase, where the introduction of negative energy particles and their influence on spacetime dynamics are critical. These dynamics, captured through modified Friedmann and big bang singularity formation, reveal that the big bang singularity disappears when Lee-Wick particles are included. Notably, negative energy particles can produce a pre-big bang thermal radiation, which occurs even in the absence of ordinary particles. This process leads to a reversible thermodynamic behavior, where the system's entropy changes monotonically, and the reversible temperature exhibits hysteresis. The interplay between the ordinary and Lee-Wick branches of the thermodynamic cycle also yields a reversible thermodynamic behavior, as the system undergoes a complete cycle without any residual effects.

Our proposed method, named StyTr$^2$, employs a transformer-based approach to perform style transfer on images. Unlike many existing style transfer techniques, ours enables the transfer of styles across different image domains, including photographs and illustrations, without requiring any additional training. We achieve this by leveraging pre-trained image and text models, specifically CLIP, which is initially used to derive style embeddings from images and generate style tokens that describe those styles. We then utilize these style tokens to refine the generation of a target image in the desired style. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique successfully transfers styles between images of distinct styles, including photographs and illustrations, while preserving the original content. Notably, the generated images exhibit high visual quality and accurately reflect the target style.

Landauer's principle is a fundamental concept linking information theory to thermodynamics, connecting the amount of information lost in an erasure process to the entropy generated by an irreversible system. In this study, we demonstrate the relationship between the rate of information loss and a system's resistance to change in a thermodynamic process. A unique property, the dissipation ratio, is identified, quantifying the minimum energy expenditure necessary to achieve a given state change. This finding confirms the optimality of a particular approach to erasure, as supported by experimental evidence using an optically connected system. Moreover, our results show that minimizing energy expenditure in an erasure process is equivalent to maximizing the efficiency of that process.

We explore the production of the top partner, $T$ quark, at an $e^{+}e^{-}e$ collider operating at $\sqrt{s}=1$ TeV with a luminosity of $1\times10^{16}$ $e^{+}e^{-}$ interactions. The $T$ quark is a vector-like quark that only interacts via fundamental strengths and its mixing with the standard model $t$ quark could resolve the electroweak minimum problem. We calculate the production of $Z$ boson decaying into $Z^{*}T\bar{T}$ through spin-1 and spin-0 $ZT\bar{T}$ vertices. The former results in $ZT\bar{T}$ production at a rate of $10^{-2}$ times the standard model $ZZ$ production rate, while the latter has a rate of $10^{-3}$ times the standard model $ZZ$ production rate. We also determine the production cross-sections of $e^{+}e^{-}ZT\bar{T}$, $A^{Z}e^{+}e^{-}e^{-}$, and $A^{Z}e^{+}e^{-}e^{+}$, which are $10^{-3}$, $10^{-4}$, and $10^{-4}$ respectively. This study explores the stability of non-uniform, non-equilibrium fluids when subjected to acoustic waves. Building on previous work, we have developed a nonlinear theory describing the interaction between these fluids and the acoustic field. Our model reveals the presence of two modes of instability, with one influenced by the fluid's shear viscosity and the other by its bulk viscosity. We have also derived a nonlinear acoustic wave speed formula and a bound on the rate of energy exchange between the fluid and the acoustic field. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of conserved quantities, with the energy of the fluid complemented by the energy of the acoustic field.

We've developed a weighted shift model on the basis of directed semi-graphs, extending the work of directed graphs by Douglas, Dirac, and Woods. This new framework allows us to investigate weighted shifts of any type, from pure to unilateral, with the possibility of generalizing existing results. Building on this foundation, we've introduced a weighted inverse method that confirms the universality of weighted shift operators. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that weighted shifts on directed semi-graphs share key properties with those on weighted graphs, such as the cyclic subproduct property and cyclic four-term factorization. In addition, we've established theorems regarding the hyperfiniteness of weighted shifts on directed semi-graphs, including generalizing the work of Jones on directed graphs.

We examine the interaction of high-energy, high-intensity lasers with high-Z targets to produce electron-positron pairs and radioactive isotopes. Using the relativistic hydrodynamics code, we model the laser-matter interaction and follow the evolution of the target's state. This investigation shows that when a high-intensity laser is directed at a target, it can generate a high-energy, relativistic gamma-photon flux, which in turn produces electron-positron pairs and induces radioactivity. The generated radiation's spectral density and flux exhibit strong correlation with the target's atomic number, while the number of produced positrons and radioactive nuclei directly depend on the photon flux. This method is expected to be utilized in the construction of compact experimental setups for producing electron-positron pairs and radioactive isotopes.

Event extraction from text involves identifying each event and its components, which is a crucial task for real-world applications. In this study, a novel approach using neural networks to extract events is presented. The proposed method first transforms raw text into a directed acyclic graph, representing events and their relationships. A neural network, specifically a graph convolutional neural network, is then used to analyze this graph and predict event types. To improve the network's performance, a new approach to generate training data is developed, utilizing a technique called syntactic significance to enhance the data. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms other event extraction methods, with improvements in F1 scores of 1.9, 2.4, and 2.7 for three different datasets.

In factor regression with errors, the hidden variables represent the true underlying factors, while the observed factor estimates are contaminated with errors. A new class of priors called error-in-factor priors has been proposed to account for these errors in a Bayesian framework, providing more accurate parameter estimates and improved posterior consistency. This research focuses on determining the geometric ergodic properties of Gibbs samplers used for error-in-factor regression, which enables reliable uncertainty quantification. A novel approach to geometric ergodicity analysis is presented, applicable to a wide range of Bayesian models, and the approach is specifically applied to error-in-factor regression, yielding geometric ergodicity for a wide range of Gibbs samplers.

We have developed a method for determining the best way to join a group of connected two-level atoms to a resonator to maximize its ability to detect low levels of input in the system. Our method uses a new mathematical approach that considers the interactions between the atoms to calculate the optimal coupling strength of the resonator to each atom. The calculation takes into account the strength of the interactions between the atoms, the frequency difference between the atoms, and the frequency difference between the resonator and the atoms. When the interactions between the atoms are strong compared to the frequency difference, our method shows that the optimal coupling strength is greater than that required for sensing without interactions between the atoms. Our method also shows that it can be difficult to determine the optimal coupling strength by simply measuring the resonator's frequency width, and that the optimal coupling strength can be determined from the frequency width measured with the atoms alone.

A novel, efficient method for solving nonlinear differential equations with random disturbances has been developed by combining the Krylov subspace technique with the Runge-Kutta method. This new approach uses the method of delayed derivatives, which is derived from the Krylov subspace, to produce a nonlinear delay vector Filling Window (DW) and corresponding delay vector autonomous differential equation. Subsequently, the Runge-Kutta method is applied to solve the DW autonomous differential equation, and the method of delayed derivatives is used to generate the numerical solution of the original differential equation with random disturbances. This proposed technique offers several advantages, including the ability to handle nonlinearity and stochastic noise simultaneously, the potential to significantly reduce the size of the DW, and the capacity to adapt to various types of nonlinearity and stochastic noise. The method's performance is demonstrated through numerical experiments that examine its accuracy and efficiency in comparison with existing methods.

This research explores a mathematical model for how light is transmitted through disordered materials, particularly those that absorb in a non-linear fashion. By utilizing Kramers-Kronig relations, a simplified model is developed that connects the real and imaginary parts of a function describing the material's optical properties. This model is derived from a more complex system governed by the vector Maxwell equations, and it is shown that it satisfies a particular set of scaling conditions. Furthermore, the model is related to a different, integral system that also predicts how light is transmitted through scattering media, and its scaling limits are characterized.

As widespread applications of machine learning have grown, there has been a growing need to understand the inner workings of these models.  This need is particularly relevant in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance, where even minor mistakes can have significant and far-reaching consequences.  While methods to explain individual predictions exist, creating models that strike a balance between performance and transparency is crucial.  This paper provides a comprehensive overview of interpretability in the context of reinforcement learning, including key approaches to understanding decision-making processes.  These approaches encompass feature-based explanations, policy explanation, counterfactual analysis, and causal reasoning, with a focus on state-of-the-art techniques in each area.  A key example illustrates how these methods can be applied to a real-world scenario, highlighting their utility in achieving transparency within critical domains.

We establish a general framework for our method, which outlines the process of creating a lattice-valued logic with one variable by utilizing a specific lattice along with its associated functions such as an evaluation map, a truth operator, a modal operator, and an accessibility relation. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our logic with one variable is equivalent to a modal equational theory derived from the specified lattice. An example illustrating this method is also included, which shows that the Sahlqvist formula class for our logic with one variable translates into a first-order theory of modal frames having a particular graph structure.

For a Gaussian process, $G_t$, in a d-dimensional space, $\mathbb{R}^d$, the deterministic signature, $\zeta_t$, of $G_t$, encapsulates the information of the trajectory of $G_t$ up to time $t$. The Wiener chaos expansion of the signature, $\zeta_t$, reveals the distribution of $\zeta_t$ within its components, and demonstrates that it is predominantly influenced by non-Gaussian components as time progresses.

In cellular networks utilizing millimeter wave frequencies, the ability of devices to switch to localized high-band connections when stronger, lower-band connections are unreliable has been proposed, but assessing this functionality requires substantial data analysis. This paper presents a statistical analysis of the impact of fine-grained network management decisions, specifically the use of localized connections based on channel quality. A simulated network model is used to study the effects of various factors on localized connection effectiveness, and how performance metrics such as user data rates are influenced by small-scale network characteristics. The study shows that even with similar average connection speeds, the rate of successful connection establishment and user data rates can vary significantly depending on specific network settings.

We provide a non-numerical proof of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a weakly interacting Bose gas in a three-dimensional trap with an intermediate strength of interactions for the following scenario. A non-zero total particle count applies, the confinement potential has a continuous derivative and its derivative is positive. In the thermodynamic limit, with interaction strength increasing, the reduced density matrix of the system converges to a two-body correlation function of the Gross-Pitaevskii wave function. This result is established using the modified Belinich-Pilat-Szocs form of the relative Hamiltonian, which is rigorously derived. Key steps in the proof include demonstrating positive definiteness of the Laplacian of the relative Hamiltonian within the GP-invariant subspace and showing that this operator remains invertible in this specific subspace.

Current image restoration methods struggle to produce detailed, high-quality images in the context of single-image processing. This is largely due to the limitations of training datasets, which are often low in resolution and don't accurately reflect the complexities of real-world scenes. As a result, existing deep learning-based solutions fall short in achieving satisfactory results. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to image restoration, which utilizes a two-phase, high-definition method to improve visual details. This technique is comprised of a series of high-resolution modules and a super-resolution module, designed to generate images with 96x1080p, 96x2k, and 96k resolutions. Furthermore, we introduce a novel loss function that incorporates the features of popular image datasets, which enables our model to learn from these datasets and produce more realistic results. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of this method in restoring both synthetic and real-world images, and even outperforms current state-of-the-art models in handling challenging, real-world scenarios.

In the context of issue-dependent priors in bandit problems, we delve into two specific challenges: binary classification with known issue classes and multi-armed bandits with known reward distributions. To address these issues, we develop and analyze several novel algorithmic approaches, each tailored to optimize a distinct objective function. Our contributions include novel thresholding algorithms for binary classification, an algorithm for multi-armed bandits that minimizes regret, and several others. We also perform a thorough computational analysis of these algorithms, comparing their performance to established methods like Thompson sampling.

In our initial paper, it was noted that an argument presented by Friedman, Linial, Saks and Sturtevant could potentially be simplified using an existing technique known as matroid compression developed by Sleator and Trevisan.

This paper proves that a hypersurface of fixed Gaussian curvature and non-negative mean curvature in the form of a horizontal graph over a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold is stable and undergoes a short flow in the mean curvature direction. We achieve this by adapting the work of Jang and Picard to our specific case. We then utilize this finding to show that such graphs are stable and possess a parabolic property.

In two-dimensional superfluids, variations in the energy cost of a pair of vortices can be expressed as a sum of Coulomb interactions involving a unique set of discrete image vortices, where the image vortices are located at the boundary of a finite region and follow a specific periodic pattern within that domain. This expression is derived from the precise solution of a boundary value problem involving the Laplace equation, and it can be used to compute the partition function of a two-dimensional system using a method that is not affected by the size of the system, and which is applicable to a wide range of system sizes.

To better understand how the average citizen perceives AI, a unique survey was conducted across eight countries. The 7-point Differential Emotion Model was used to analyze responses to questions about AI's past impact, present influence, and future potential. The results reveal intriguing contradictions - while people generally have positive feelings towards AI, they are equally concerned about its potential risks. The nations surveyed, including China, France, India, Japan, Mexico, the UK, and the US, showed similar patterns of concern for AI's impact as it becomes more prevalent. However, when considering AI's future potential, emotions shifted towards more positive outcomes such as excitement and wonder. The study suggests that as AI becomes more embedded in daily life, both the immediate challenges and long-term consequences will need to be addressed to fully harness its potential.

The first branching ratio measurement of the inhibited decay $\Xi_c^0\to\pi^-\Lambda_c^+$ is conducted using a dataset from the BESIII detector, corresponding to 2 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected in $e^+e^-$ collisions at the $\sqrt{s}$ PUMSS. The obtained branching ratio is compared to the decay $\Xi_c^0\to\psi K^-$, and the two decays are used to study $\Xi_c^0$ hadronization. The measured branching ratio of $\Xi_c^0\to\pi^-\Lambda_c^+$ is $1.0\times10^{-2}$, with a relative uncertainty of 6.8%.

We establish a method for estimating the stable component of the product of two operators within the confines of Banach algebras. This framework is further adapted to address a type of functional equation characterized by quadratic terms.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is a common method found in robotics and related fields. However, the exploration process in this method can be improved by using a statistical technique. This study demonstrates how the application of a statistical technique, specifically Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, can enhance the performance of actor-critic reinforcement learning, specifically in terms of exploration. Additionally, the research presents empirical results showing the effectiveness of combining Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with actor-critic reinforcement learning on various environments.

We investigate a complex quantum model consisting of three coupled components: an active atom, a cavity, and environment. This system can be represented by a mathematical equation with three parts that together describe the behavior of the Dicke model in a three-part system. To better understand the system's overall state, we use a specific mathematical approach to find its energy levels. Next, we analyze the system's stability under different conditions using a method that considers its energy levels. Our analysis shows that the system exhibits a range of stable states when it's near a specific threshold of energy, including states with unique properties that enable perfect quantum processing. Furthermore, the system shows a transition from one stable state to another when the system's energy parameters change, and we also find that the system's behavior at certain points is characterized by unusual stability and other interesting features.

In many real-world multi-agent reinforcement learning environments, collaborative agents can benefit from working together, such as accountants and tax inspectors. However, standard MARL methods often fail to produce optimal group outcomes due to being self-focused. To overcome this, we've developed a novel approach called CoMTL, a framework that enables agents to learn from one another by sharing knowledge. By integrating a transfer agent with level-adaptive reward distribution, we've created a dynamic system where agents collaborate more effectively, resulting in better overall performance. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our method, particularly in dynamic settings, outperforming traditional transfer learning approaches in various scenarios.

This research introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning environment for a particle robot that navigates and manipulates objects in a simulated 2D space. The objective is to utilize deep reinforcement learning to enable the particle robot to navigate to predefined target locations while carrying and moving small objects around static obstacles. Building on prior research, this approach expands the scope of controlling the particle robot with deep reinforcement learning to encompass object transportation and introduces an environment where the robot can interact with small objects in a complex setting.

Using the CRIAS instrument at the Telescopio de Canarias, we conducted an investigation into the atmospheric composition of the hot Jupiter exoplanet WASP-31b. We employed a novel method that involves monitoring the changes in light as the exoplanet transits the star and compares it to similar data from other planets. This allowed us to identify a consistent pattern in the abundance of certain elements. Our analysis revealed that WASP-31b contains an abundance of sodium and magnesium, but surprisingly lacked potassium. This discovery aligns with predictions made by theoretical models suggesting that the exoplanet's atmosphere is dry.

High-performance computing as a service offers the advantage of allowing users to access and deploy applications with various memory requirements. However, the service typically forces users to work within the computing platform's set memory limitations. Persistent memory, on the other hand, can offer the necessary memory expansion to fulfill high demand. It also provides the advantage of being non-volatile, thus eliminating the need for frequent data retrieval from storage. The integration of persistent memory into high-performance computing as a service infrastructure could thus provide users with more flexibility. Our paper explores the benefits of incorporating persistent memory into HPCaaS for users, as well as the challenges that cloud providers face in offering such an infrastructure.

To better understand the human brain, researchers utilize classification techniques on fMRI data to pinpoint different areas of the brain that respond to various stimuli. While existing methods typically compare individual brains to achieve population-based classification, these methods have certain limitations. In response, we've developed a novel approach that leverages the unique characteristics of multiple brains to inform a more accurate classification. By creating a graph that connects individual brains and another graph for each fMRI volume, we've developed a framework that combines these insights to improve classification results. In our study, we've tested this approach on an fMRI dataset and found it to be highly effective.

This research examines the Gauss sum formula within the frameworks of classical complex numbers, quaternions, and octonions, then adapts it to the realm of octonion geometry, where it is reinterpreted as an invariant volume measurement for certain spherical polytopes. The paper goes on to calculate Gauss sums for specific polytopes, including the tetrahedron, the triangular prism, and two types of spherical triangular prismatic polytopes. Additionally, a formula is devised to determine the Gauss sum of any given pyramidal polytopes, supported by examples of various spherical pyramids. Finally, the Gauss sum formula is reinterpreted, this time within the context of octonion braid theory, where it is seen as a distinct invariant for braid equivalences.

In this research, we have measured the angular dependence of the critical angles for Cherenkov radiation in thin films of beryllium and silicon, both in the super-critical range. The experimentally obtained data were then compared to both theoretical predictions from the theory of total reflection and simulations based on Monte Carlo methods. The results from the theoretical predictions showed a satisfactory match with our experimental findings, whereas the Monte Carlo simulations provided a less accurate fit. Notably, our study has provided the first direct evidence of gentle Cherenkov radiation in the context of X-ray total reflection, an phenomenon previously only documented in water solutions.

In this research, we tackle the task of implicit argument identification and labeling for Universal Cognitive Architecture Synthesis (UCCA). We introduce a novel approach, combining a pre-trained model with a specialized algorithm to generate high-quality, syntactically accurate annotations, thus addressing this challenge for UCCA. Our proposed method is adaptable to various approaches that analyze syntax to some extent. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in significantly enhancing the accuracy of implicit argument labels, with a notable gain of 21.9% in F1 score over the baseline approach.

A common method in weakly supervised learning uses certain areas of an image to indicate what should be classified. However, traditional approaches require humans to label these areas, which isn't practical for large image datasets like those containing chest X-rays. Our research introduces an autonomous method that identifies and labels these areas using existing medical images and their corresponding labels. These regions are then used to train a multiple instance learning model for classifying and locating diseases in chest X-rays. Our approach outperforms previous methods by significantly improving performance across multiple benchmarks.

In machine learning and statistics, model selection is a crucial problem that has been addressed using various criteria, including the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and its modified version, the AICc. However, these criteria are susceptible to variations in sample sizes, particularly when working with limited data. This paper introduces a new model selection criterion, the minimum penalized Hellinger divergence, which is derived from the Hellinger distance and offers a more robust estimate of expected model log-likelihood. Notably, the proposed criterion consistently selects the best model under specific conditions. In simulations involving finite sample sizes, the proposed criterion outperformed AIC and AICc in model selection, particularly when sample sizes are limited. This approach has practical applications in bioinformatics, demonstrated by its use in identifying the best model for quantifying genetic variation.

The Prouhet-Thue-Morse word $\omega_1$ derived from the sequence $\varepsilon_{2^n}$ where $\varepsilon_i = 1 - 2^{-i}$, has a fixed binary pattern that appears at specific positions. Each digit of this word can be represented as a sum of binary rational fractions. We define binary motifs as a pattern of these fractions at the ends of certain words. Given the fixed nature of the Morse sequence and its corresponding binary words, our research focuses on the upper bound of the length of the binary motifs within the word $\omega_1$. We demonstrate that this upper bound is $k+1$ and that it can be achieved by examining the binary motifs of length $k+1$ in the word.

In applications requiring dynamic choice, a model must select from multiple options based on the current situation. Prior studies on classifier grouping or selection models for dynamic choice focused on straightforward models but overlooked the impact of price factors on group selection. This paper proposes a new formal framework for dynamic choice that incorporates price sensitivity in classifier choice. We introduce a novel algorithm, Price-sensitive Hierarchical grouping with Softmax (PHS), which groups classifiers hierarchically and uses a non-parametric approach to model price effects. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms other options, including a baseline based on expert opinions.

The Tianlai project, which includes the 7m radio telescope and 7m interferometer, as well as the upcoming 30m telescope, will conduct a comprehensive cosmological survey spanning the redshift range of $0.5-3.7$. This document outlines a detailed processing system that will enhance the detection sensitivity of the 7m telescope through advanced calibration and imaging techniques, validated by real experimental data. Furthermore, the paper presents a dedicated pipeline for extracting the spectrophum MCM-MC method-based cosmological power spectrum from the 7m interferometer data. This pipeline is unique in that it can simultaneously estimate the power spectrum in the entire observed field without requiring a reference field for self-calibration, offering the potential for precise large-scale structure measurements. This paper serves as an introduction, technical specifications, and initial performance testing of the pipeline, as well as a demonstration of its functionality using real data.

To explore potential applications in spintronic devices, we investigate the magnetic properties of VSi2N4, NbSi2N4, and VSi2P4 monolayers through density functional theory calculations. Our findings show that these compounds exhibit significant differences in their magnetic behavior, with the ferromagnetic phase of VSi2P4 displaying the lowest energy and exhibiting the highest magnetic stability. Ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic arrangements result in distinct magnetic moments for these compounds, with VSi2PimN4 displaying the largest magnetic moment of 1.54 Bohr magnetons, surpassing the Landau-Lifshitz limit. Notably, the Curie temperatures of these materials are substantial, suggesting their viability for spintronic applications. Our study also reveals that the magnetic exchange couplings in these materials are an order of magnitude greater than transition metal dichalcogenes like CoO, WO, and WTe2.

Gneiting and Lutkemeyer's 2006 findings indicated that positive definite kernels in metric spaces can be reduced to invariant functions of distance, based on properties derived from the spectral filter. Building upon their discovery, this paper introduces a novel, direct method for constructing positive definite kernels from scratch, allowing for the creation of new invariant kernels in metric spaces. This method makes only two key assumptions: the existence of certain kernels and a specific symmetry in their interactions. Our novel kernels offer advantages in terms of their smoothness, and this has practical implications for their applications.

For a positive semigroup S on a countable set X, we investigate the definition and implications of atomicity, which essentially means that the non-trivial elements of S can be divided into distinct, irreducible parts. Our research focuses on the properties of atomic semigroups, particularly their relationship with subsemigroups and quotient semigroups, as well as the linear nature of their associated generating functions. Additionally, we create a new class of complex plane functions that allow for a detailed analysis of their zeros, and use this framework to design a semigroup recognition algorithm.

In medical research, identifying the potential benefits of exposure in the presence of confounding variables can be complicated. To address these challenges, we've developed a straightforward approach to estimate the attributable fraction among exposed using case narrative data. This method involves creating synthetic data by drawing samples from a Bayesian propensity score model, which is used to generate these samples. The proposed method then utilizes bootstrapping to calculate the variability within each generated dataset and produces multiple estimates of the attributable fraction among exposed. By combining these individual estimates, we can provide a reliable estimate of the attributable fraction among exposed while minimizing the influence of unwanted biases. A simulation study was conducted to compare our approach with existing methods, and real-world data were used to further validate its effectiveness.

Let $k$ be a field where zero-cycles can be defined. The set of zero-cycles generated by morphisms from smooth projective varieties over $k$ to an abelian variety over $k$, divided by equivalence relations such as Poincaré duality and finite surjectivity, forms algebraic groups. We demonstrate the existence of these zero-cycles in all possible classes. Furthermore, with the additional assumption that the base field $k$ has characteristic zero, the base field can be replaced with an algebraically closed subfield, known as the field of a standard variety. Consequently, the motivic Galois group of this subfield acts continuously on these groups, which are referred to as standard varieties.

A study was conducted of the $\Upsilon$(1S), $\Upsilon$(2S), and $\Upsilon$(3S) mesons that were produced through radiative decay, and which were detected in the $\Upsilon$ $\to$ $\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decay channel by the CMS experiment at the LHC. The results, which were obtained after analyzing 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ worth of data collected at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, are presented in relation to the transverse momentum of the $\Upsilon$ mesons and the number of charged particles in the events measured. The results for the cross-sections of $\Upsilon$(1S), $\Upsilon$(2S), and $\Upsilon$(3S) mesons that are produced in relation to the transverse momentum of the $\Upsilon$ mesons are consistent with the predictions of next-to-leading order QCD. However, the cross-sections of $\Upsilon$(2S) and $\Upsilon$(3S) mesons that are produced in relation to the transverse momentum of the $\Upsilon$ mesons follow a power-law distribution with a slope of $-7.00$. However, the cross-sections of $\Upsilon$(1S) mesons that are produced in relation to the transverse momentum of the $\Upsilon$ mesons follow a power-law distribution with a slope of $-6.92

In this study, we explore the concept of strongly connected quantum dots and propose a model consisting of a central dot connected to four surrounding dots via Coulomb coupling, which allows for a range of exciton states to emerge. Utilizing a master equation approach, we develop a set of rate equations to model the exciton states' temporal behavior, and subsequently solve them to derive the steady-state exciton density matrix. Subsequently, we apply the properties of the density matrix to determine various entropy measures, including von Neumann entropy, R\'enyi entropy, and conditional entropy, which provide insights into the system's exciton state state. Our results demonstrate the influence of the system parameters on these measures, shedding light on the inherent exciton state of the system.

The Geometric Modulus Theorem is a finding that relates to the relationship between the values of an entire function at its critical points, providing insight into the function's behavior. This note explores how the theorem's boundaries are defined by the holomorphic and harmonic functions within the theorem's scope.

We have examined the stability of bright solitons within a discrete nonlinear Schrodinger model, taking into account both short-range and long-range interactions. The research focused on a chain of $L$ sites with a repulsive short-range potential and a weak long-range attraction, expressed mathematically as a dipole-dipole interaction in the form of a $1/r^3$ relationship. By analyzing the linear stability of bright solitons using the semi-analytical steepest descent method, we found soliton stability for smaller values of $\beta$ but a critical point at $\beta \approx 0.34$. Below this critical value, bright solitons remained stable, while above it, they became unstable and eventually collapsed.

This research focuses on developing a unified approach for applying majorization-marginalization techniques to optimize geometric and signomial functions. Building upon previous research, we establish necessary conditions for optimality in geometric and signomial optimization, which facilitate the use of majorants based on log-sum-exp functions. We also derive multi-concave majorizing functions for geometric and signomial functions, enabling the development of MM algorithms for efficiently solving various problems in these areas. Specifically, we provide a generic algorithm for minimizing geometric functions subject to box constraints, with linear and superlinear convergence. We also provide a general framework for optimizing signomial functions with box constraints, achieving superlinear convergence. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach by presenting a signomial minimizer grounded in majorization-marginalization and achieving linear convergence. We also showcase the practical applications of our method in two specific areas: nonnegative rate function learning and signomial regression.

Following an earlier study, the Teichmuller manifold's global Torelli property is re-examined with a broader scope of Teichmuller geodesic segments. Based on the ergodic theory of the Teichmuller vibration operator, a proof is developed to show that the Torelli property persists even when considering any collection of Teichmuller geodesic segments.

Recent advancements in neural radiance fields and neural point fields have led to significant improvements in representing 3D characters with real-time capabilities. Although existing methods have achieved remarkable results in capturing detailed character shapes and details from photogrammetry data, they often require a dense set of measurements, which can be expensive and impractical to obtain. This research presents a novel approach, referred to as PINA, that generates a customized implicit 3D character model from a single RGB-D video stream. By leveraging the latest implicit neural rendering techniques, PINA can efficiently capture complex 3D shapes and animations from a single video, even in the absence of a large dense sequence. To further enhance the accuracy of the resulting model, a novel deformation-based regularization method is introduced, which leverages the temporal variations in the video to optimize the model's reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of PINA, showcasing its ability to generate high-fidelity 3D characters from a single video in real-time.

Recent advancements in generative adversarial networks have led to impressive results in image inpainting. However, when working with face images, existing methods struggle to maintain facial structure and produce realistic outcomes. This paper introduces a novel method that leverages a 3D morphable model to preserve facial features and generate more authentic results. By utilizing parameter codes from a 3D morphable model, our model can reconstruct face shapes, and a corresponding generator can create face textures based on the input image and code. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in maintaining facial structure and producing better outcomes than direct image inpainting, and more promising than texture inpainting, in terms of both structural integrity and realism.

A new approach to reinforcement learning, called intrinsic-driven learning, has been developed by modifying traditional algorithms to prioritize intrinsic rewards over external ones. This reformulation, which emphasizes maximizing return on its own, has the advantage of being independent of the agent's environment and can be applied universally to any environment. Intrinsic-driven learning has been successfully applied to various agents, including single and multi-agent configurations, and has led to improved results in areas such as curiosity-driven learning and self-play in games.

A multi-agent Markov decision process (MARP) with connected nodes provides a suitable framework for studying cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning problems. This paper focuses on the state-action reward interface (SARI) model, which combines the strengths of state-based and state-action-based models. We show that with the presence of a 'root node,' the agents can collaboratively achieve the optimal joint policy by utilizing a distributed learning algorithm. This algorithm relies solely on local information and inter-node connections, and it satisfies specific conditions. These conditions include the requirement for sufficient connectivity and the absence of certain graph configurations, which are essential for ensuring global convergence. Our analysis builds upon the concept of positive algebraic connectivity, which is rooted in the works of Li, Lin, and Ma.

The occurrence of events featuring two leading jets and a significant gap in rapidity between them is examined in high-energy proton-proton collisions. This analysis utilizes data from the CMS detector at the LHC, with a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV and a corresponding data sample of 5.1 fb$^{-1}$ in integrated luminosity. Two distinct methods for identifying these events involve analyzing the distribution of events with two leading jets in terms of differential jet transverse momentum and the probability of observing such events within a specific window in rapidity. Both methods reveal a consistent change in trend at approximately 5.0 and 3.4 TeV in jet transverse momentum and rapidity gap, respectively, indicating a possible double-particle exchange process.

Silicon, an extensively researched element due to its exceptional electronic and mechanical properties, has garnered significant attention following the successful creation of silicene, a low-dimensional silicon structure. Researchers have investigated the thermoelectric potential of penta-silicene, a ring-shaped silicon structure with five atoms in each unit cell, and found it to possess a distinctive phase diagram under ambient conditions, featuring an insulating state at low temperatures and a degenerate Fermi liquid at high temperatures. The latter exhibits unusual transport characteristics, including a large Seebeck coefficient and a significant electrical conductivity, as well as the presence of two distinct charge carriers with opposite signs. Consequently, the figure of merit of penta-silicene appears to be highly dependent on temperature and field conditions. The results suggest that penta-silicene could be a promising material for thermoelectric applications due to its high performance and the potential to fine-tune its performance through adjustment of temperature and applied field.

We have investigated the impact of a magnetic field on the ground and excited states of heavy quarkonia when they exist in a non-relativistic environment with fractional dynamics. Our model calculations for the binding energies and magnetic field-induced shifts in these states will enable us to compare our results with available experimental data.

We have conducted extensive research into the interactions of dark matter particles with a wide range of massive objects across the universe, encompassing stars, galaxies, and other celestial bodies. By applying our numerical code to these objects, we have generated a detailed understanding of dark matter scattering behavior, which we believe is crucial for determining the rotational periods of nearby neutron stars. Additionally, we have developed a new analytical framework to predict the distribution of dark matter velocities, which we have applied to a variety of space-based experiments. This new framework allows us to more accurately model the detection signals from these experiments, which specialize in identifying dark matter particles through their collisions with nucleons. Furthermore, we have applied our findings to ancient Earth and other rocky celestial bodies, which we believe could potentially serve as sensitive detectors for dark matter particles.

This study focuses on how agents in a decentralized system can cooperate and confess their actions to a central entity when faced with uncertainty about their actions. We develop a framework where agents compete with each other and against a number of fake agents to maximize their rewards for truthfully reporting, while the system tracks the total rewards for all truth-telling agents. We analyze the learning dynamics when the system and the agents use different learning methods, specifically when the system uses an optimal algorithm and the agents use a basic learning method. We also investigate how the system's rewards change in this case, and provide additional results on the effectiveness of the decentralized system compared to a centralized system.

Recent advancements in deep reinforcement learning have led to the successful application of robots in diverse environments, particularly in complex tasks that are difficult to program. However, the performance of DRL algorithms can be compromised by noisy observations, a problem that is often overlooked in the evaluation process. Moreover, the need for extensive simulation to fine-tune these algorithms limits their effectiveness in real-world settings. Our proposed solution, TERP, addresses these challenges by leveraging a probabilistic approach to enhance the reliability of DRL-based planners and developing a simulation framework that utilizes real-world data to facilitate fast and accurate simulation. Our results demonstrate that TERP achieves a 50% improvement in reliability when compared to conventional DRL algorithms and successfully navigates obstacles in the lab with a success rate exceeding 99.8%, backed by successful real-world deployments.

The global phase portrait of a specific type of three-dimensional dipole model has been examined using phase portraits obtained numerically to identify the stable and saddle points, as well as the asymptotic solutions. A Lyapunov function has been proposed to classify the linearized equations near the saddle points and confirm a significant result regarding the source locations in this model.

The goal of this research is to determine the location, shape, and alignment of an insulating object within a flat surface using direct current measurements on the surface and voltage readings on a circular boundary around the object. Initially, this problem is transformed into a Fredholm integral equation form. Next, this equation is solved using the general method for inverting integral equations. This method involves expanding the solution using an appropriate basis set, which is formed by combining singular functions and coordinate translations. Numerical simulations demonstrate the accuracy of this approach, showing that it can accurately detect the insulating object's location even when surrounded by noise.

The stability of toroidal magnetic fields in stars is considered, with the equation determining this stability modified to include terms representing the decrease in magnetic field due to turbulent mixing and the induction effect caused by convective motion. It is found that in a certain region of the star's core, toroidal magnetic fields may stabilize and increase, whereas in another area they are subject to oscillations that can cause the magnetic field to collapse. This oscillation can be suppressed by turbulent mixing and convective effects.

This research delves into the intricate topological and geometric properties of complex networks and computational systems, particularly those with a hierarchical or modular structure. The work begins by examining the underlying topological characteristics of biological systems, focusing on the modular coordination within the Drosophila melanogaster brain's network. The analysis reveals that the brain's network consists of multiple interconnected components, and by comparing the resulting topology with that of random networks, researchers can identify the most critical features that define its architecture. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the brain's network achieves optimal coordination when its computational components, or 'algebras,' are well-organized and integrated into the system. Building on this discovery, the investigation explores the relationship between geometry and topology in the context of algebras, which ultimately leads to the development of a novel framework for describing and analyzing modular structures and their associated coordination patterns. The proposed framework is then applied to various systems, including the brain, social networks, and cellular networks, and the results provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between geometry, topology, and coordination.

Sparse matrix multiplication is a crucial operation in numerous linear algebra applications, particularly in sparse matrix-based systems. SpMV plays a central role in iterative solutions of large linear systems, underscoring its importance. Given that SpMV is computationally expensive, it is essential to optimize its performance. This research delves into the current advancements on SpMV acceleration and proposes innovative techniques, including the implementation of a binary search method to locate matrix elements efficiently. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through benchmarking on the University of Florida Sparse Matrix Collection. The findings reveal that the proposed approach can yield substantial speedup compared to the current fastest SpMV algorithms, particularly for sparse matrices with large dimensions. The techniques developed in this research can be seamlessly integrated into various computing platforms, including CPUs, GPUs, and MIC processors, and the associated source code is available for free.

Let's consider two groups of meromorphic functions over the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, with $G_1$ being a subset of $G_2$. It can be proven that if a certain condition is met, where the forward images of zero, along with the forward images of any finite number of its nonzero values, are shared among the functions in $G_2$, then the functions in $G_1$ are normal within the sense of Montel, thus yielding new insights with relatively minimal additional requirements.

Advancements in AR hardware are creating new opportunities for social interaction to evolve, yet the potential impact on human relationships remains a topic of debate. This study examines how individuals' intentions to engage with others might influence the effectiveness of wearable AR devices. A novel, non-invasive approach was developed to detect when someone is attempting to interact with a nearby person using their AR headset. The approach was validated through a large-scale experiment involving 32 participants and demonstrated an accuracy rate of 92.5%, along with other promising results.

This research paper introduces novel Monge-Ampéere frameworks inspired by novel concepts in symplectic geometry. Our primary objective is to develop a theoretical foundation that allows the simultaneous and interconnected study of two models. By utilizing a unified approach, we have formulated a master equation that establishes a direct correlation between the two models. Additionally, we have formulated a total energy balance equation, which not only governs the evolution of the potential for one model but is also interconnected with the potential for the other model. To establish these theories, we have expanded the principles of homotopy and Liouville capillarity.

The initial stages of electrodeposition involve mass transfer from a solution to a growing crystal or film, accompanied by gas evolution, which can lead to bubble formation on the surface. This bubble growth disrupts the smooth deposition process, and its timely removal is crucial to avoid serious problems. To address this, researchers have employed computational modeling to explore the influence of natural convection on bubble size and behavior, and how this affects their adhesion to the electrode. The study demonstrates that as bubbles grow, they become more easily detached from the surface due to their increased buoyancy. The simulations also reveal that forces such as surface tension and contact angle play a key role in this process, and the understanding gained can be applied to various contexts, including electrodeposition.

A search was conducted for long-lived charginos and neutralinos, the byproduct of stop decays, in collisions between protons at the LHC. This study utilized data from the CMS detector, totaling 36.3 fb^-1 of events at 13 TeV, to investigate the potential of delayed photons as a distinctive indicator of long-lived particles. To achieve this, a novel method was implemented, requiring the detection of two photons with one exhibiting anomalous timing. The results were then compared to standard photon candidates. The standard photons were categorized into three groups, referred to as signal regions, based on the timing difference between the photons, denoted as Delta t. The research focused on scenarios where chargino and neutralino lifetimes were comparable, with masses of 300 GeV for the chargino and 55 GeV for the neutralino. The results indicated that chargino and neutralino masses of 740 GeV and 640 GeV, respectively, were excluded at the 95% confidence level, with stop masses of 1 TeV. The research also explored the possibility of detecting long-lived particles in upcoming experiments, with a predicted 95% confidence level exclusion range of 1.7 TeV for the stop Higgs boson, 1.8 TeV for the wino neutralino, and 1.9 TeV for the stau neutralino. The research also set a new benchmark for the minimum mass of the neutralino

Recent research has identified a new class of Dirac semimetals, such as CaSb2 and Na2Sb. These semimetals are distinct from well-known Ta-N and Pt-Co materials in that their electronic properties are near the Fermi level. This study examines the impact of Coulomb interactions on second-order Dirac semimetals within the context of weak coupling. By utilizing a renormalization group method, we found that the coupling between Dirac fermions and bosons is significant and the scaling behavior of the critical exponent is characteristic of a unique bosonic condensate. This study provides an explanation for the observed quantum oscillations in the heat capacity and magnetic field-dependent behavior in second-order Dirac semimetals.

Designing concurrent programs is a complex task that demands strategic organization of multiple threads.  The way data is structured plays a significant role in achieving efficient concurrency.  Existing tools for automatic generation of concurrent programs from sequential data organization specifications fall short in effectively providing solutions.  This is largely because they fail to adequately account for the nuances of concurrent programming.  This paper presents a novel approach, based on answer set programming, to derive a concurrent program from a sequential data organization specification.  The method is structured around two stages: initial generation of potential concurrency solutions, followed by refinement of these solutions to ensure they align with the desired data organization specification.

A novel method for testing the gravitational field and universal gravity constants is being developed, utilizing a non-gravity-dependent sensor based on superconducting magnetic levitation. By suspending a superconducting coil above a superconducting sheet, the sensor can detect and compensate for residual motion caused by gravity. A key challenge in the technology lies in achieving stable levitation, and our approach presents an optimized platform and control system that enables long-term and portable sensor operation. With further development, the proposed technology has the potential to provide high accuracy (10^-15) and spatial coverage (0.1 m) in measuring the gravitational field, thereby facilitating the detection of new physics in the gravitational field.

Cyclopentadiene, a compound with five carbon atoms and triple bonds, has been identified in space for the first time. Detected in the TMC-1 region, the molecule's two distinct forms, 1-EtC$_5$H$_3$CCH and 2-EtC$_$_5H$_3$CCH, were identified through their rotational lines. These forms were predicted to have similar energy levels and initial assumptions were made about their relative abundance. Observations revealed that the two forms have almost equal intensity, with estimated relative abundances of approximately 0.34 to 0.66, indicating their total abundance is roughly 0.34 to 0.66 parts per million. This finding is consistent with the presence of a chain of chemical reactions, where acetylene leads to the formation of benzene, but the exact mechanism of this process has yet to be determined.

The CMB measures energy density at the time of decoupling, equating to a weighted average of the dark matter density along the line of sight. The density variations, known as isocurvature perturbations, can be used to measure the local dark matter density variations. The Planck collaboration found the local dark matter density to be 0.267 with a margin of error. In the context of a cosmological model with dark matter that interacts across large distances via gravity, the density of dark matter can be unevenly distributed. The unevenness in dark matter density translates to a variation in the CMB and a corresponding variation in the measured gravitational potential. The measured CMB and gravitational potential variations are related through the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect and Bessell's potential, allowing us to calculate the local dark matter density and compare it to the Planck collaboration's findings. The calculated density is 0.26 with a margin of error, with a margin of error for the change in the Bessell potential of approximately 0.02.

Using 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data from the LHC, which was collected by the ATLAS experiment at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV between 2015 and 2016, t$\bar$tZ production was investigated. The t$\bar$tZ production rate was determined to be 1.1 (1.4) pb at a 95% confidence level within three distinct t$\bar$tZ signal regions. The t$\bar$tZ production rate was found to be consistent with the predicted Standard Model cross-section of 1.02 (0.98) pb.

We introduce a classification of four-qubit states based on a specific categorization of entanglement types. Our analysis categorizes four-qubit states into categories based on their unique entanglement properties. Our investigation reveals that the four-qubit states can be grouped into six distinct classes: one class of states that can be represented as three two-qubit pure states, and five classes of states that can be represented as two two-qubit pure states in different combinations of product basis systems. Our research further identifies specific examples of four-qubit maximally entangled states, and four-qubit GHZ states that can be assigned to these six classes. Additionally, we explore the geometrical structure defined by the set of four-qubit states, and specifically identify the properties of each class within this structure.

We introduce a general approach to dynamic games that harmonizes the incentives of individual players by transforming these incentives into a simplified representation of predictive state representations. This representation of predictive state representations enables us to develop a range of strategies for games with multiple players, including those with limited information and mixed strategies. We establish that certain properties of this simplified representation ensure a balanced game, leading to a limited set of possible outcomes. We illustrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a specific game, and the resulting solution achieves optimal results.

Gentrification, the gradual transformation of a local community due to the influx of wealthier residents and rising property prices, is a widespread phenomenon in cities worldwide. In the United States, gentrification typically involves the displacement of low-income and minority residents who are forced to abandon their neighborhoods. Research into gentrification's causes and effects is limited due to the lack of standardized data collection methods. This study aims to address this issue by developing a systematic approach to tracking gentification patterns in cities. A proposed data-driven system utilizes machine learning to identify early warning indicators of gentrification in Buffalo, New York. This novel system's development and implementation serve as a model for cities globally, offering insights into the challenges and benefits of this approach.

The controlled movement of magnetic skyrmions within host paramagnons enables their use in memory technology and data processing technology. Their stability and mobility are significantly influenced by the crystal structure and strain within the material. To fully understand skyrmion motion, researchers must be aware of the intricate relationships between crystal structure, magnetic arrangement, and strain within the material. This study examines the unique phase transitions within the Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ alloy, observing the transformation from a skyrmion lattice to a helical state as the system is heated. Through the use of high-resolution X-ray diffraction, researchers measured the thermal expansion of the material and utilized the resulting data to calculate the material's strain state. This information was then used to calculate the magnetic arrangement and confirmed these results with neutron scattering. This approach provides a clear understanding of the magnetic arrangement and phase transitions within the material. The findings suggest that the phase transitions within the alloy are driven by a gradual change in the material's strain state, leading to the gradual melting of the skyrmion lattice.

Consider the Hardy space on the n-dimensional unit ball $\mathbb B^n$ as defined by Stegeman and view it as a canonical Besov space on $\mathbb B^n$. Forming operators on harmonic spaces within function classes is a well-established concept, with existing research including those on harmonic Besov spaces. Building on this understanding, we introduce formation operators on harmonic Bloch-type spaces and examine various topics such as inequalities, domination, parallel sums, and dual spaces within this context.

The growth in electric vehicle usage is likely to be followed by a surge in range extended electric vehicles (REVs), which offer reduced battery costs. However, the increased demand for charging Revs by electric vehicles (EVs) at bordering stations may lead to congestion. This study proposes a method to determine the most efficient routes for both traditional and range extended vehicles to minimize congestion, and demonstrates its effectiveness in a comprehensive network of 30,000 intersections within New York City. The results indicate that the percentage of time EVs spend at Rev charging stations can be reduced from 13.4% to 2.5% without compromising on travel time.

We compute the distribution magnitudes of heavy-light and heavy-annotated mesons, as well as quarkonia, within the light-front framework. By employing a Gaussian heavy quark approximation in the heavy quark's momentum representation, we derive a universal function that governs heavy meson distributions, which can be extended to heavy-annotated mesons. This function is then adapted for heavy-annotated mesons, resulting in distribution magnitudes that exhibit dependence on the heavy quark mass. Our approach is further applied to heavy-annotated quarkonia, where the heavy quark is considered as a heavy quark within a quark. The results show that heavy quark masses have a significant impact on distribution magnitudes.

In models describing transients, the velocity law is frequently employed, but it has a significant drawback, as it fails to comply with the mass balance equation. This leads to an inaccurate model that amplifies transient periods at the expense of simulation accuracy, particularly when the system is close to equilibrium. This paper proposes the Enhanced Velocity approach, designed to mitigate this limitation. By integrating the velocity law with the enhanced oil rate and storage capacity concepts, the Enhanced Velocity method allows for more accurate simulation of transient periods. We examine the effectiveness of this method through a comparative analysis with a standard velocity simulation.

The widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles relies heavily on computer vision, a critical component in their functionality. Current computer vision models are often evaluated using static, 2D image datasets, which may not fully represent real-world scenarios. To fill this knowledge gap, we develop a framework that assesses models' performance in dynamic, spatial environments, enabling them to learn from complex vision-based information. Our evaluation method involves testing models on sequences of 3D spatial data, which capture the temporal variations in real-world traffic situations, offering a more accurate representation of reality. To create these spatial data streams, we combine 2D image encodings with 3D spatial information, enabling models to leverage both spatial and temporal context. Our analysis examines how models' perceptions of their surroundings influence their performance, which is then used to identify areas for improvement.
